text: Ankylosaurus was a low, wide plant-eater covered in bony armour. At the end of its tail was a heavy club of fused bone. By swinging its tail from side to side, it could hit with a lot of force.

Scientists think the club could break a leg bone. Tests on [[fossil|fossil]] clubs, and healed injuries on a close relative, suggest it was used both against [[predator|predators]] and in fights with other ankylosaurs. A blow aimed low, at the shins of a two-legged hunter, would have been the most dangerous.

st.prompt: What stopped Ankylosaurus's tail from flopping about when it swung the club?

options.t: Stiff, bony rods along the end of the tail, like a handle
Extra muscles packed inside the club
A shell that covered the whole tail

st.reveal: The bones near the end of the tail were locked together by tendons that had turned to bone. That made a stiff handle, so the heavy club at the tip could be swung from the hips, like a hammer.

src: Royal Ontario Museum, Zuul crurivastator.
Arbour V.M. (2009) Estimating impact forces of tail club strikes by ankylosaurid dinosaurs. PLoS ONE 4.
n.certNote: Tests and healed injuries show the club could deliver a heavy blow. Whether it was used mostly on predators or on rivals of its own kind is still debated.

It had no shell. Its back was covered in hundreds of separate bony plates set in the skin, a bit like a crocodile's back, so its body could still bend.

sec.t:
Ankylosaurus lived at the very end of the [[@dino-age-span|age of dinosaurs]], in the same places as [[@trex-bite|T. rex]]. It was about as long as a minibus and probably weighed more than an elephant. It was low to the ground, with short legs and a body almost as wide as it was long.

Its back, neck and head were covered in [[osteoderm|osteoderms]]: plates and knobs of bone that grow inside the skin. [[@croc-ancient|Crocodiles]] have them too, which is why a crocodile's back feels knobbly. Some of its relatives even had a plate of bone in each eyelid. Its belly, though, had no armour.

In 2017, scientists described an ankylosaur from Montana with an unusually complete skeleton, including its skin armour. They named it Zuul crurivastator, after a monster in the [[@hollywood|film]] Ghostbusters. The second name means "destroyer of shins".

In 2022, the same team looked closely at Zuul's sides. Several spikes along its flanks were broken and had healed. The damage was in places that another ankylosaur's swinging tail would reach. Big hunters would more likely bite the back or neck. So the clubs seem to have been used in fights between ankylosaurs, perhaps over mates or space, like rams butting heads.

Being covered in bone has a cost. It is heavy, and Ankylosaurus could not have run fast. Instead, it relied on being very hard to bite. A predator that grabbed its back would get a mouthful of bone.

This is a different plan from [[@stegosaurus|Stegosaurus]], which lived tens of millions of years earlier and carried long spikes on a flexible tail. Ankylosaurs did not have their clubs from the start either. Early members of the family had armour but plain tails. The full club, with its stiff handle, appeared later, as if the family slowly improved one weapon.

The first Ankylosaurus bones were found in Montana in 1906 by Barnum Brown, the same fossil hunter who found [[@trex-montana|the first T. rex skeleton]]. Even now, Ankylosaurus itself is known from only a few partial skeletons. Much of what we know about the club comes from its better-preserved cousins.

text: Around the time of the [[asteroid|asteroid]], huge cracks in western India poured out [[lava|lava]] again and again. The flows piled up more than 2 km thick.
These stacked flows are called the Deccan Traps. "Trap" comes from an old Swedish word for stairs. Look at the step-shaped hills of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]].
The volcanoes released gases that changed Earth's [[climate|climate]]. Some scientists think this made life harder before the asteroid hit. Others think it mattered much less.

keys.cap: Long cracks open in western India. Runny lava floods out and spreads in flat sheets.

keys.label: Layer on layer
keys.cap: Eruption after eruption. Each sheet of lava cools into a new layer of black rock called basalt.

keys.label: 66 million years ago
keys.cap: The asteroid strikes Mexico. In India, the eruptions keep going.

keys.label: After
keys.cap: The lava pile grows more than 2 km thick and covers a huge part of India.

keys.label: Today

quiz.reveal: The caves of Ajanta and Ellora, and the Elephanta caves near Mumbai, were all cut into Deccan basalt. At Ellora, the Kailasa temple was carved downwards from the top of a single hill of lava rock.

n.certNote: The eruptions are proven. How much they helped kill the dinosaurs is still argued about.

myth: The Deccan eruptions came from tall, cone-shaped volcanoes like Mount Fuji.
Most of the lava poured out of long cracks in the ground and spread out in flat sheets. There was no single giant mountain. The layers piled up into a thick plateau instead.

sec.t:
These weren't volcanoes like a mountain with a [[crater|crater]]. Lava gushed from long cracks and flooded the land in sheets, layer after layer. [[geologist|Geologists]] call this a flood basalt. Some single flows were large enough to run hundreds of kilometres.

Between eruptions there were quiet spells, sometimes long enough for soil to form and plants to grow. These in-between layers, called intertrappean beds, hold [[fossil|fossils]] of plants, frogs, fish, snails and insects. They show that life carried on in the gaps, until the next flood of lava arrived.

As India drifted north, it passed over a hot spot deep in Earth's mantle, the same hot spot that today sits under Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean. Hot rock rose from deep below like a blowtorch under a moving sheet of metal. [[@india-drift|See India's route]].

The eruptions may have helped India move too. Some scientists think the rising hot rock pushed India along faster for a while, making it one of the fastest-moving landmasses known.

Here is the puzzle. The [[@extinction|asteroid]] struck Mexico 66 million years ago. The Deccan eruptions had begun before that and carried on after it. Both happened within the same short slice of time, geologically speaking.

Volcanoes release [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], which warms the planet over thousands of years. They also release sulphur gases, which can cool it quickly by blocking sunlight. If large pulses came before the asteroid, they might have stressed life already. In 2019, two teams dated the lava very precisely. One found a big pulse of eruptions just before the impact. The other found that most of the lava came out after it. Both studies were published in the same issue of the same journal, side by side.

Most scientists agree the asteroid was the main killer. The open question is whether the Deccan Traps made things worse, and by how much.

{{story:ellora-kailasa}}

Much of Maharashtra and parts of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka sit on Deccan basalt. The dark rock is strong and easy to carve, which is why ancient artists chose it for the caves of Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta. The [[@ellora-kailasa|Kailasa temple]] at Ellora was cut from a single basalt hill. Many forts in the Sahyadri hills, built by the [[@marathas|Marathas]] and others, stand on flat-topped basalt ridges with steep cliffs on every side, ready-made walls left by the old lava.

The black basalt rock weathered into the rich black soil of the Deccan plateau, great for growing [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]]. Farmers call it regur, or black cotton soil. It holds water well and cracks wide open in the dry season.

The layers also made the step-like hills of the Western Ghats. Dinosaurs like [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]] walked across this land just before and during the eruptions, and some of their bones lie in rock just below the lava.

text: We don't know yet. So far, the only place in the universe where we know life exists is Earth. But scientists are now searching more seriously than ever, in three main ways.

They are exploring places in our own [[solar-system|solar system]] where tiny living things, like [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]], might survive, such as Mars and the icy moons of [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] and Saturn. They are studying the air of planets around other stars for gases that life might make. And some are listening for radio signals that an intelligent [[civilisation|civilisation]] might send. Any one of these could one day change the answer from "we don't know" to "yes".

st.prompt: Which of these places did NASA's Cassini spacecraft find spraying water into space?

options.t: Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn
Earth's Moon
The planet Mercury

st.reveal: In 2005 Cassini spotted jets of icy spray shooting from cracks near Enceladus's south pole. Flying through them later, it found salt, organic chemicals and other ingredients life could use, all coming from a hidden ocean.

src: NASA Astrobiology Program.
SETI Institute.
n.certNote: No life beyond Earth has been confirmed. Scientists disagree about how common life is likely to be, and several exciting claims, such as gases on Venus or K2-18b, are still being argued over.

d.try: With an adult, put a teaspoon of dried yeast and a teaspoon of sugar into a clean bottle with a little warm (not hot) water. Stretch a balloon over the neck and wait half an hour. The balloon slowly inflates with gas made by the living yeast. Scientists search other worlds for signs like this, gases that living things give off.
myth: UFO sightings prove that aliens are visiting Earth.

No sighting has ever produced solid evidence of alien visitors. Most turn out to be planes, balloons, satellites, the planet Venus or tricks of light. A 2023 NASA study panel found no evidence that any unexplained sightings came from beyond Earth.

liquid water, energy, the right chemicals

sec.t:
On Earth, every living thing needs liquid water, a source of energy and certain chemicals, especially ones built around carbon. Life also turns out to be tough. [[microbe|Microbes]] live in boiling [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]], in rock kilometres underground and in [[@earth-weird-blood-falls|Antarctic ice]]. Whole communities thrive around [[@deep-sea-vents|hot vents on the deep sea floor]], far from any sunlight.

So scientists look for places with those ingredients, even if they look nothing like Earth's meadows and forests.

There are more than 6,000 known planets around other stars, and probably hundreds of billions in our [[galaxy|galaxy]]. Some are rocky and the right distance from their stars for liquid water.

[[@telescopes-how|Telescopes]] like the James Webb Space Telescope can now study the air of some of these planets. In 2025, one team reported a possible hint of a gas on a planet called K2-18b that, on Earth, is made mostly by living things. Many other [[astronomer|astronomers]] think the evidence is too weak, and further studies have not settled it. Arguments like this are exactly how science tests big claims.

In 1960, the American astronomer Frank Drake pointed a radio telescope at two nearby stars for a few weeks, listening for messages. He heard nothing, but he started [[@mystery-wow-signal|SETI]], the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence. A year later he wrote down an [[@equations|equation]] listing all the things you'd need to know to estimate how many civilisations might be out there.

In 1977, a radio telescope in Ohio picked up a strong, short signal that so excited the astronomer on duty that he circled it and wrote "Wow!" in the margin. It has never been detected again, and its source is still unknown. That is the point: one strange signal is not proof.

Around 1950, the physicist Enrico Fermi reportedly asked his colleagues at lunch: if the galaxy is so huge and old, where is everybody? Nobody has a settled answer. Perhaps life is rare. Perhaps it is common but intelligence is rare. Perhaps the distances are simply too vast.

Scientists think about this using [[@probability|probability]], weighing what we know against what we don't. For now, the honest answer is that the universe hasn't told us yet.

text: The night sky is dark because the universe had a beginning, and because it is expanding.

Light travels fast, but not instantly. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so light from very distant stars and [[galaxy|galaxies]] simply hasn't had time to reach us. We only see stars in a limited bubble around us, and in between them, the sky looks black. On top of that, the universe is stretching. Light from the farthest galaxies gets stretched as it travels, shifting it into colours our eyes can't see, and making it fainter.
This simple question, why is it dark at night, turns out to be one of the clues that the universe isn't eternal.

st.prompt: If there are billions and billions of stars, why isn't the night sky filled with light?

options.t: The universe had a beginning, so light from the farthest stars hasn't reached us yet
Dust in space blocks the light
There aren't really very many stars

st.reveal: Light takes time to travel, and the universe is about 13.8 billion years old. So we only see light from a limited region. Dust doesn't solve the puzzle, because if starlight kept shining on it for ever, the dust would heat up and glow too.

src: NASA, Cosmic Microwave Background.

myth: The sky is dark at night simply because the Sun has set.

That explains why our side of Earth is in shadow, but not why the sky between the stars is black. In an endless, unchanging universe full of stars, every direction would end on a star and the whole sky would shine. The darkness needs a deeper explanation.

sec.t:
Picture standing in a huge forest. If the forest goes on far enough, every direction you look ends at a tree trunk. You can't see past them.

[[astronomer|Astronomers]] in the 1600s and 1700s realised the same should be true of stars. If space went on for ever, filled evenly with stars, and had always existed, then every line of sight would eventually end on the surface of a star. The whole sky would be as bright as the Sun's surface, day and night. The German astronomer Heinrich Olbers wrote about this in 1823, and the puzzle is named after him, though others raised it earlier.

Some people suggested that dust between the stars blocks the light. But dust soaking up starlight for long enough would heat up until it glowed as brightly as the stars.

The real answer came slowly. Surprisingly, one of the first people to describe it was the American writer Edgar Allan Poe, in an essay in 1848. He suggested that the sky is dark because light from the most distant stars has not yet had time to arrive.

In the 20th century, astronomers discovered that galaxies are rushing apart and that the universe began with the [[@big-bang|Big Bang]]. Light from beyond a certain distance hasn't reached us yet. When we look far away, we look back in time, as explained in [[@light-years|light-years]]. Look far enough and we see back to when there were no stars at all.

The sky between the stars isn't completely dark. In 1964 and 1965, two radio astronomers in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, kept picking up a faint hiss with their antenna, coming from every direction. At first they thought it was caused by pigeons nesting in the antenna. They cleaned it out, but the hiss stayed.

It turned out to be the afterglow of the Big Bang, light released when the universe was about 380,000 years old. Over billions of years, the stretching of space has turned it into faint microwaves, a kind of [[@radio-waves|radio wave]]. Penzias and Wilson won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978. If your eyes could see microwaves, the whole sky would glow dimly.

text: Nobody knows, because we haven't found any aliens yet. But scientists aren't completely in the dark. Life on Earth has [[evolve|evolved]] for about 4 billion years, and it keeps solving the same problems in similar ways. Many scientists think alien life, if it exists, would follow some of the same rules.

That means aliens might have features that work well anywhere: ways to sense light, move, find food and avoid danger. On the other hand, a planet with stronger [[gravity|gravity]], thicker air or a different star would shape life in its own way. And the most common aliens are probably tiny [[microbe|microbes]], not creatures you could shake hands with.

st.reveal: On Earth, life was made only of single cells for about 3 billion years before animals appeared. Most scientists think microbes are far more common in the universe than complex creatures, and they are what our probes and telescopes are most likely to find.

n.certNote: No alien life has ever been found, so everything here is educated guessing. Scientists base their ideas on how life evolved on Earth, but they disagree about how much that tells us.

Decide how your creature moves, eats, senses things and stays safe. Then explain each choice using an animal on Earth that does something similar.
myth: Aliens probably look like humans, with two arms, two legs and big heads.

Human-like aliens are mostly an idea from films, partly because actors in costumes are human-shaped. Life on other worlds would evolve to suit its own conditions, and could look very different from us.

sec.t:
The planet itself would shape aliens. On a world with strong gravity, animals might be short, wide and sturdy, with thick legs. On a low-gravity world, they could grow tall and spindly, and flying would be easier.

Thick air would make flying and gliding simpler, and sound would carry well. A planet around a dim, red star might have plants that look very dark, even black, to soak up as much light as possible. NASA scientists have modelled this using what we know about [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] on Earth.

Aliens might not live on the surface at all. Moons like Europa and Enceladus have huge oceans hidden under ice. No sunlight reaches them, but life might feed on chemicals from the seabed, as it does around [[@deep-sea-vents|deep-sea vents]] on Earth. Creatures there could look like the tube worms, pale crabs and glowing fish of our own deep oceans.

Saturn's moon [[@titan|Titan]] is stranger still. Its lakes are filled with liquid methane, at about minus 180 °C. Some scientists wonder whether life could use methane instead of water, with chemistry completely unlike ours. Nobody knows if that's possible.

The classic "grey alien", with a big head, large black eyes and a small body, comes mostly from science fiction and stories from the 1960s onwards. Film aliens are often human-shaped because actors had to wear the costumes.

Real aliens would have no reason to resemble humans. Even on Earth, most animals don't. More than a million insect [[species|species]], sponges, jellyfish and [[fungus|fungi]] show how many different shapes life can take.

Intelligent aliens, ones that could build radio telescopes, would need some way to handle objects, like hands, tentacles or trunks. They would need senses to understand the world and a way to communicate, perhaps with sound, light, colour patterns or chemicals.

On Earth, intelligence evolved separately in apes, dolphins, crows and octopuses, so it may not be unique. But it took about 4 billion years to produce a species that builds rockets. We don't know if that's typical or very rare.

In 1977, NASA's two Voyager probes set off carrying a message for any aliens who might find them, with greetings, music and pictures of people. No one knows if anyone will ever see that [[@space-golden-record|golden record]]. If they do, they may find our shape just as strange as theirs would seem to us.

text: Space itself has no smell, because it is nearly empty. A smell is made of tiny bits of a substance floating in air, and your nose catches them. Out in space there is almost no air and almost nothing to catch.

But astronauts keep noticing something odd. When they come back inside the [[@space-station|International Space Station]] after a spacewalk and take off their helmets, their suits and tools give off a strong scent. They describe it as hot metal, seared steak or welding fumes. Nobody is fully sure why. Out in the rest of the universe, telescopes have found clouds and planets that, in theory, would smell of rum, raspberries and rotten eggs.

st.prompt: Apollo astronauts brought Moon dust into their lander on their suits. What did they say it smelled like?

Fresh rain on dry soil
Nothing at all

st.reveal: Several Apollo astronauts said the grey dust smelled like spent gunpowder. Moon dust contains no gunpowder at all. One idea is that the sharp, never-weathered grains reacted with the damp air inside the cabin.

n.certNote: Many astronauts have described the smell, so it is real. Why it happens is still argued over, and the main ideas have not been fully tested.

Space is almost a perfect vacuum, so there is nothing for your nose to catch. Taking off a helmet would also be deadly. The smells astronauts describe come from their suits and tools once they are back inside, where there is air.

sec.t:
The station has an airlock: a small room where air is pumped out before a spacewalk and pumped back in afterwards. Once the air returns, the crew smell it. Former NASA astronaut Don Pettit wrote that it reminded him of a sweet, metallic smell, like welding. Others have said it is like the smell of a hot engine.

One popular idea is that the outside of a [[@spacesuits|spacesuit]] picks up loose oxygen [[atom|atoms]] in [[orbit|orbit]]. Up there, sunlight splits oxygen into single, very jumpy atoms. When they meet the cabin air, they may form [[ozone|ozone]], which has a sharp, electric smell. Another idea is that surfaces simply get very hot in sunlight and very cold in shadow, which can make metals release odd smells. Both ideas are still guesses.

sec.h: A galaxy that smells of rum
sec.t:
In 2009, [[astronomer|astronomers]] using a radio telescope studied Sagittarius B2, a huge cloud of gas and dust near the middle of our [[@milky-way|Milky Way]]. They found ethyl formate there. On Earth, this chemical is part of what makes [[@berries|raspberries]] taste like raspberries, and it smells a little like rum.

You would never get to sniff it. The cloud is about 26,000 light years away, and it also contains poisonous chemicals. Still, it is a strange thought: some of the same [[molecule|molecules]] in your fruit bowl drift between the stars.

sec.h: Rotten eggs at the edge of the solar system
sec.t:
Not every space smell is nice. In 2018, scientists using the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii found hydrogen sulfide in the clouds of [[@uranus-sideways|Uranus]]. That is the gas that makes rotten eggs stink. A visitor would not have time to complain, though. Uranus is colder than minus 200 °C and its air is mostly hydrogen and helium.

[[comet|Comets]] can be smelly too. The Rosetta spacecraft followed comet 67P for two years from 2014. Its sensors found hydrogen sulfide, ammonia and hydrogen cyanide around the [[@comets|comet]]. Scientists joked that 67P smelled of rotten eggs, a horse stable and bitter almonds.

Astronauts in training have sometimes been given samples of a "space smell" made on Earth by a chemist who copies scents. The idea is to stop the real thing from surprising them up there. And the oddest part? Astronauts often find their food tastes dull in orbit, because floating body fluids stuff up their noses. Without a working [[@nose-smell|nose]], even a spicy curry starts to taste like cardboard.

text: The Moon's [[gravity|gravity]] pulls on everything on Earth, including the oceans. It pulls hardest on the side of Earth facing it, so the water there piles up into a bulge. On the far side, the Moon pulls the water least, and a second bulge forms there too.

As Earth spins, each coast passes through both bulges. When your beach is inside a bulge, the sea creeps up the sand. That is high tide. When it is between bulges, the water slides back. That is low tide. Most coasts get two of each every day.

[[@sun-what|The Sun]] pulls too, but less than half as strongly, because it is so much further away. [[@moon-tides-life|When the Sun and Moon line up]], they team up for bigger tides. The pull even stretches the solid ground. The rock under your feet rises and falls by a few tens of centimetres every day, too slowly and smoothly for you to notice.

frames.cap: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, making the water bulge towards it.

As Earth spins through the bulges, the sea rises and falls about every 12 hours and 25 minutes.

sec.h: Why the tides come later each day
sec.t:
High tides don't come at the same time each day. They arrive about 50 minutes later. That is because while Earth spins, the Moon keeps moving along its path around us. Earth has to turn a little extra to catch up, so the gap between high tides is about 12 hours and 25 minutes.

Fishermen, sailors and port workers live by these times. In India, the Survey of India prints [[@charles-babbage|tide tables]] for ports such as Mumbai, Kolkata and Kandla, so ships know when there is enough water to sail.

In the open ocean, the tide only rises by about a metre. But in long, narrow bays, the water gets squeezed and piles up much higher. The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the biggest tides on Earth, up to about 16 m, as tall as a five-storey building.

India's biggest tides are in the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat, where the sea can rise and fall by several metres. Nearby, at Lothal, people of the [[@indus-cities|Indus civilisation]] built a large brick basin over 4,000 years ago. Some [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] think it was a dock that let boats in on the high tide. Others think it held water. They still disagree.

In some rivers, the rising tide rushes upstream as a single wave called [[@ocean-tidal-bore|a tidal bore]]. The Hooghly near Kolkata has one, and so does the Qiantang River in China.

sec.h: A forest that floods twice a day
sec.t:
In the Sundarbans, the tide floods the [[@mangroves|mangrove]] forest twice a day and drains it again. The trees grow breathing roots that poke up out of the mud, and even the [[@sundarbans-tigers|tigers]] there are strong swimmers.

The tides are slowly changing our planet too. Their drag acts like a gentle brake on Earth's spin, making each day longer by about two thousandths of a second every hundred years. At the same time the Moon is drifting away from us, about 4 cm a year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

text: [[@ants-world|Some ants]] grow fungus, some herd insects, and some build homes with [[@glue-sticky|living glue]].

Leafcutter ants have been farming for tens of millions of years. Humans began [[@farming-began|farming]] only about 12,000 years ago. Ants were already around with the dinosaurs, and some are trapped in 99-million-year-old [[@amber-fossils|amber]].
Farming ants don't plan the way people do. Each ant follows simple rules, set off by smells and touch. But a whole colony, working together, manages its crops as carefully as any farmer.

spots: Fungus farmers
Leafcutter ants in South America carry leaves home, not to eat, but to grow fungus gardens they eat.
Weaver ants (India!)
Red weaver ants glue leaves together into nests, using silk from their own larvae like glue sticks.
Ant ‘cows’
Some ants guard aphids and ‘milk’ them for sweet honeydew.

quiz.prompt: Leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaf back to their nest every day. What do they do with them?

options.t: Eat the leaves for dinner
Use them to grow a fungus, which they eat
Line their nests to keep warm

quiz.reveal: Leafcutter ants can't digest leaves. They chew them into a mash and use it to feed a fungus garden underground. The fungus grows special swollen tips, and those are what the ants and their young eat.

d.try: Watch ants at work. Put a few grains of sugar and a crumb of biscuit near an ant trail outside, then sit quietly for ten minutes. Notice how the first ant to find food goes back, and how more ants soon follow the same path. Gently draw a line through the trail with your finger and watch how they search to find it again.
myth: The queen ant is the boss who gives orders to the rest of the colony.
The queen lays the eggs but doesn't give orders. The workers, all female, make decisions together using smells and touch.
facts: tens of millions of years ago

sec.t:
In the [[@rainforests|rainforests]] and dry scrub of Central and South America, and as far north as Texas and Louisiana in the USA, leafcutter ants march in long lines. Each worker carries a piece of leaf above her head like a green sail.

The leaves don't get eaten. Underground, smaller workers chew them into a pulp and spread it in chambers as [[compost|compost]] for a special [[fungus|fungus]]. The fungus grows, and the ants eat its swollen tips. The ants weed their gardens, pull out unwanted moulds, and even carry [[bacteria|bacteria]] on their bodies that make natural medicines against pests. A big colony can hold millions of ants, with fungus gardens spread through hundreds of chambers.

When a young queen leaves to start a new nest, she carries a tiny piece of fungus in a pouch in her mouth. It's the seed for her colony's first crop.

{{story:mushrooms}}

Aphids are tiny insects that suck sap from plants. They squirt out a sugary liquid called honeydew. Many ants love it. Some ants stroke the aphids with their antennae to make them release a drop, a little like milking.

In return, the ants guard their "herds" from ladybirds and other hunters. Some carry aphids to fresh plants, or shelter their eggs in the nest over winter. Gardeners in India and the USA often notice that where there are lots of aphids, there are lots of ants. Some ants go further. Certain [[species|species]] in Asia carry mealybugs, another sap-sucking insect, with them when they move house, like herders driving cattle to new pasture. The ants and their "cattle" can depend on each other so completely that neither does well alone.

In [[@mango-tree|mango]], cashew and other trees across India, red weaver ants build nests by stitching leaves together. Workers line up along a leaf's edge and grab the next leaf with their jaws. When the gap is too wide, they hang onto each other to make [[@power-ant-bridges|a living chain of bodies]] and pull the leaves close.

Then other workers bring [[larva|larvae]], the ants' young, and squeeze them gently. The larvae give out silk, and the workers dab it back and forth like a glue stick until the leaves are sewn tight. Weaver ants are fierce defenders and eat many insect pests. In parts of Asia, farmers have welcomed them into fruit orchards for centuries.

In Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, some communities make a sour, spicy chutney from red weaver ants and their eggs. In 2024, the red ant chutney of Similipal in Odisha received a Geographical Indication tag.

Ants live alongside many other insect partners. Fig trees have their own [[@fig-wasps|wasps]], and termites, which are more closely related to cockroaches than to ants, grow fungus gardens of their own inside their mounds. Farming has been invented at least three times by insects, long before people tried it.

text: Pure water freezes at 0 °C. Salty water has to get colder than that before it freezes. Scientists call this freezing point depression.

On a winter road, the top of the ice is always coated with a thin film of liquid water. When salt [[dissolve|dissolves]] into that film, it makes salty water, which can stay liquid below 0 °C. The salty water eats into the ice around it, which makes more salty water, and the ice slowly turns to slush. Snowploughs can then push the slush away, and [[@tyres|car tyres]] can grip the road again.
Salt works best when it's not too cold. Below about minus 10 °C, ordinary rock salt struggles, and road crews switch to other chemicals or to sand and grit.

st.prompt: You mix crushed ice with a big handful of salt in a bowl and put a thermometer in it. What happens to the temperature?

options.t: It rises above 0 °C, because the ice melts
It drops well below 0 °C
It stays at exactly 0 °C

st.reveal: As the salt makes the ice melt, the melting soaks up heat from the mixture, so it gets colder, down to around minus 20 °C. That's how people froze ice cream and kulfi long before home freezers.

d.try: Put an ice cube in a glass of water and lay a piece of thread across its top. Sprinkle a pinch of salt over the thread and wait about a minute. Gently lift the thread. The salty water re-freezes around it, and the cube comes up with it.
myth: Salt melts ice by heating it up.

Salt doesn't add heat. It lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so ice that touches salt starts to melt even below 0 °C. The melting soaks up heat, so the salty slush actually becomes colder than the ice was.
facts: salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes
Rock salt works well down to about −10 °C
Road salt used in the USA
often more than 20 million tonnes a year
rusts cars and bridges, harms rivers and roadside plants

sec.t:
When water freezes, its [[molecule|molecules]] lock together into a neat, six-sided pattern of ice crystals. That's also why [[@why-ice-floats|ice floats]]: the pattern takes up more space than liquid water.

Dissolved salt breaks into tiny charged particles that get in the way. They make it harder for water molecules to line up and join the crystal. So the water has to be colder before it can freeze. The more salt, the colder it has to get, down to about minus 21 °C for the saltiest possible mixture.

Sea water, which is salty, freezes at about minus 2 °C. That's why the ocean around Antarctica can stay liquid when the air is far below freezing.

The same science that clears roads can [[@ice-cream-freezing|freeze a dessert]]. When salt is mixed with crushed ice, the ice starts melting. Melting needs heat, which it takes from its surroundings, so the mixture gets much colder than plain ice, down to around minus 20 °C.

For centuries, cooks in India set kulfi in cone-shaped metal moulds packed into earthen pots of ice and salt. The milk mixture froze solid in the extra-cold slush. Before home freezers, American families made [[@ice-cream|ice cream]] in a hand-cranked churn the same way, with a bucket of ice and rock salt around a metal can.

Salt is cheap and works, but it causes problems. Salty water speeds up [[@rust|rust]] on cars, bridges and the steel inside concrete. As snow melts, the salt washes into streams, lakes and groundwater. The US Geological Survey has found rising salt levels in many rivers in the northern USA, which can harm fish, frogs and plants.

Cities are trying to use less, by measuring roads' temperature, spreading only what's needed and using more brine. In the high Himalayas of India, where passes freeze for months, road crews depend more on snow-clearing machines and closures than on salt. Every icy road is a balance between safety today and cleaner water tomorrow.

text: A good forger can copy every brushstroke of a famous painting. What they can't easily copy is time. Paint, canvas and wood change over the centuries in ways that scientists can measure.

Scientists who study and care for paintings are called [[conservator|conservators]]. They use [[@x-rays|X-rays]], [[microscope|microscopes]] and chemistry to look at the hidden layers of a picture. If a painting claims to be 300 years old but contains a paint invented 80 years ago, the game is up.
These same tools also show how famous artists worked: the sketches under the paint, the changes of mind, and sometimes a whole different picture hidden underneath.

spots: X-rays
X-rays see through top layers. Sometimes they show a sketch, or a totally different painting, hidden underneath.
Paint that's too new
Some pigments were only invented recently, like titanium white (about 100 years ago). Find it in an ‘ancient’ painting, and it's fake.
Microscopes
Tiny cracks, dust and brush hairs show how old the paint really is.
Carbon dating
Wood and canvas came from living things, so their age can be measured with atom clocks.

quiz.prompt: A painting is signed and dated 1700. Scientists find titanium white in it. What does that tell them?

options.t: That paint can't have been put on in 1700
The painter was far ahead of his time
Nothing, because all white paint is the same

quiz.reveal: Titanium white was only sold as an artists' paint from about the 1920s. So either the painting is a fake, or someone repainted part of it later. Experts check exactly where the paint sits to decide which.

src: National Gallery, London, Scientific Department, National Gallery Technical Bulletin.

d.try: Make a hidden picture. Draw a simple shape on white paper with a white wax crayon or a candle stub, pressing hard. Then brush watery paint over the whole sheet. The wax pushes the paint away and your secret drawing appears, a bit like the hidden layers that scientists reveal in old paintings.
myth: Carbon dating tells you exactly when a painting was painted.

Carbon dating measures when the plants in the canvas or wood stopped growing, not when the paint went on. A forger can paint on an old canvas, so scientists combine carbon dating with tests of the paint itself.
facts: from nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s
smaller than a grain of salt

sec.t:
X-rays pass easily through canvas and most paints, but not through [[@art-materials|heavy pigments]] such as lead white. So an X-ray photo of a painting shows where the artist laid on thick, lead-rich paint, much as a hospital X-ray shows bones.

[[@cameras-how|Infrared cameras]] see through the top layers to the charcoal sketch beneath. Under [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light, old varnish glows a milky green, while recent touch-ups look like dark patches.

Scans of [[@picasso|Pablo Picasso]]'s *The Blue Room*, made from 2008 onwards, revealed a portrait of a bearded man in a bow tie hidden underneath. Picasso was young and poor when he painted it in 1901, and canvas cost money. So he simply painted over an earlier picture.

{{story:x-rays}}

Every [[pigment|pigment]] has a birthday. Prussian blue was first made in Berlin in the early 1700s. Titanium white went on sale as an artists' paint around the 1920s. Bright modern blues and greens called phthalocyanines arrived in the 1930s.

So scientists take a speck of paint, smaller than a grain of salt, and test what it is made of. A painting signed 1650 with titanium white in it cannot be genuine. This simple rule has caught many forgers, because they buy their paints in modern shops.

Old Indian paintings have a timeline too. The painters of [[@ajanta-colours|Ajanta]] used earth colours and lapis lazuli, so a modern factory-made blue in a "Mughal" miniature is a warning sign.

Canvas is woven from flax or cotton, and panels are cut from trees. Both were once living plants. Living things take in a type of carbon, carbon-14, that slowly breaks down after they die. Measuring how much is left gives an age, using the same [[@half-life|half-life]] trick that dates ancient bones.

There's a twist. Nuclear bomb tests in the 1950s and 1960s added extra carbon-14 to the air. Plants that grew after that carry a tell-tale "bomb peak". In 2019, scientists in Switzerland found it in threads from a painting that claimed to be from the 1800s, proving the canvas was woven a century later. Wooden panels can also be dated by counting their tree rings.

Most of the time, art scientists aren't hunting fakes at all. They are working out how to protect paintings from light, damp and dust, and how to clean them without harm. Under a microscope, tiny cracks called craquelure show how paint has dried and shrunk over many years.

In India, labs at museums and at the Archaeological Survey of India use similar tools to care for wall paintings, palm-leaf [[manuscript|manuscripts]] and miniatures. For the human side of the hunt, with its forgers, fooled experts and courtroom drama, read about [[@art-forgery|how experts spot fake paintings]].

text: The [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] in Rajasthan gets little rain, and only during the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. In the far west, near Jaisalmer, a whole year's rain can be less than 25 cm, while summer days often pass 45 °C.

For centuries, people have survived by saving rainwater cleverly, in tanks, ponds and [[@india-wonder-chand-baori|stepwells]]. They built thick-walled houses, herded animals that could cope with [[drought|drought]], and grew hardy crops like bajra, a kind of [[@millets|millet]].
The golden city of Jaisalmer is built from local yellow sandstone. Rocks of the same region hold [[@dino-feet-tracks|dinosaur footprints]], left long before there was any desert at all.

spots: Camels
Camels can go days without drinking and walk easily on sand. They're called ships of the desert.
Stepwells
Deep wells with steps going down to the water, like Chand Baori in Rajasthan, with about 3,500 steps.
Cool houses
Thick walls of stone or mud keep heat out in the day, and small windows block hot winds.
Catching rain
Round covered tanks called kunds catch every drop of rain and store it for months.

quiz.prompt: About how many steps lead down to the water in Chand Baori stepwell?

options.t: About 3,500
About 35
About 35,000

quiz.reveal: Chand Baori, in the village of Abhaneri near Jaipur, has about 3,500 narrow steps in criss-cross patterns down 13 storeys. It was built more than a thousand years ago, so villagers could reach water even when the level dropped deep underground.

d.try: Fill two identical cups with the same amount of water and mark the levels. Cover one with a plate and leave the other open, both in a sunny spot. Check every day for a week. The open cup loses more water to evaporation, which is why desert people built covered tanks called kunds.
myth: Deserts are just empty sand dunes where nothing lives.

Only part of the Thar is shifting dunes. Much of it is scrubland with thorny trees, grasses and farms. It is home to blackbuck, desert foxes and the rare great Indian bustard, and to millions of people.
facts: about 2 lakh km², in India and Pakistan

sec.t:
The Thar covers about 2 lakh km², mostly in Rajasthan, with parts in Gujarat, Haryana, Punjab and Pakistan. Many deserts around the world are almost empty. The Thar is one of the most crowded, with towns, villages and farms scattered across it.

Part of the reason is that it gets some rain each year, unlike the driest deserts. Another is that people here learned, over hundreds of years, how to make every drop count.

The desert is also full of colour. Women wear bright odhnis and heavy silver jewellery, and men wear tall turbans in reds, oranges and yellows. Folk singers called Manganiyars and Langas have sung ballads of desert kings and lovers for generations, often for the same families their ancestors sang for.

The [[@camels|camel]] has been the Thar's truck, tractor and taxi for centuries. It can go days without drinking, carry heavy loads and walk on soft sand with its wide, padded feet. Rajasthan made it the state animal in 2014.

Herding communities such as the Rabari move with their camels, goats and sheep to find grazing. Every year, [[@india-wonder-pushkar|the town of Pushkar]] on the desert's edge holds one of the world's largest camel fairs.

Desert houses have thick walls of stone or mud that soak up the day's heat slowly, so rooms stay cooler inside. Small windows keep out hot winds and blowing sand. Courtyards give shade.

In Jaisalmer, carved stone screens called jaalis let breezes through while blocking the glare. Jaisalmer Fort, a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], is one of the few forts in the world where thousands of people still live.

[[@wild-blackbuck|The Bishnoi community]] of the Thar protects trees and animals as part of its faith. [[@deer-india|Blackbuck and chinkara deer]] often wander fearlessly near Bishnoi villages. Their story of sacrifice at Khejarli in 1730, to save khejri trees, later inspired India's [[@chipko|Chipko]] movement.

Since the 1950s, the Indira Gandhi Canal has carried water from rivers in Punjab hundreds of kilometres into the desert. Fields of wheat, cotton and mustard now grow where there was once only scrub. It changed many lives, though it also brought problems, such as waterlogged and salty soil in some places.

text: Spices like [[@cardamom-pepper|pepper]], cardamom and cinnamon were among the most valuable goods in the ancient world. [[@food-pepper-black-gold|Black pepper]] grows on vines in the forests of the Western Ghats, in [[@kerala|Kerala]], and for centuries India was its main source.

The [[@monsoon|monsoon]] winds made long sea voyages possible, connecting India with Africa, Arabia, Rome and China. Traders who controlled the spice routes grew rich, and later, European countries sailed around the world trying to reach India's spices directly.
Ideas travelled with the spices: numbers, foods, stories, religions and inventions. The search for pepper helped shape [[empire|empires]], and even led Europeans to the Americas by accident.

frames.cap: Black pepper grows on vines in the forests of the Western Ghats, in Kerala.
Over 2,000 years ago, sailors learned to ride the monsoon winds across the Arabian Sea, to India in summer, back home in winter.
Roman traders paid with gold coins. Thousands have been found in South India!
Much later, in 1498, Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to reach Calicut. Countries raced to control the spice trade.

quiz.prompt: In 1667, a peace treaty let the English keep Manhattan, in today's New York, while the Dutch kept Run, a tiny island in Indonesia. What was Run famous for?

options.t: Nutmeg
Black pepper
Cinnamon

quiz.reveal: Run was one of the few places on Earth where nutmeg grew, and nutmeg was worth a fortune in Europe. The Dutch thought they had the better deal. Today Manhattan is one of the most valuable pieces of land in the world.

d.try: Collect five spices from your kitchen, such as black pepper, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and dried chilli. Smell each one, then find out where it first grew. Mark the places on a world map. You will find that chilli, now everywhere in Indian food, came from the Americas only about 500 years ago.
myth: In the Middle Ages, Europeans bought spices mainly to hide the taste of rotten meat.
Historians say this is unlikely. Spices cost far more than meat, so people rich enough to buy pepper could also afford fresh food. Spices were prized for flavour, medicine and showing off wealth.

sec.t:
More than 2,000 years ago, sailors learned to ride the [[monsoon|monsoon]] winds [[@ocean-currents|across the Arabian Sea]]. From about June, the wind blows from the south-west, pushing ships towards India. From about November, it turns and blows from the north-east, carrying them home.

A Greek guidebook for traders, written in the first century CE and called the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, describes [[@sea-ports|ports]] along India's coast and what each one sold. Pepper, [[@pearls|pearls]], ivory, cotton cloth and precious stones all went west.

Ships and [[caravan|caravans]] carried more than goods. Indian numbers, including the idea of [[@zero-invent|zero]], travelled west through Arab traders and later reached Europe. Buddhism spread along land and sea routes to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China. The game of [[@chess-india|chess]], which probably began in India, travelled to Persia and on to Europe.

Overland, the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] linked China, India and the Mediterranean, and many spices went that way too.

For centuries, Arab and Venetian merchants controlled the spice trade into Europe, and prices there were very high. European rulers wanted to cut them out.

In 1492, Christopher [[@columbus|Columbus]] sailed west hoping to reach Asia, and landed in the Americas instead. In 1498, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and landed near Calicut, in Kerala. Soon Portuguese, Dutch, English and French ships were fighting to control the trade.

The English [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] was founded in 1600 to trade in Asian spices. Over the next 250 years, it moved from trading to ruling, and took control of much of India.

The Dutch focused on the "Spice Islands" of Indonesia, where nutmeg and cloves grew. They used great violence to keep control, including against the people of the Banda Islands.

Trade worked both ways. Portuguese ships brought chillies, potatoes and tomatoes from the Americas to India. Within a few centuries, chilli was so common in Indian cooking that it is hard to picture a curry without it. Pepper, once worth its weight in silver, now sits on almost every dining table in the world.

text: The US [[economy|economy]] is the largest in the world, worth about 30 trillion dollars a year in 2025. It works mainly as a market economy. That means most things are made and sold by private businesses, and prices are set mostly by [[@supply-demand|supply and demand]] rather than by the government.

Ordinary shoppers drive it. About two-thirds of the economy is households buying things: food, rent, phones, doctors' visits, streaming services, holidays. Businesses spend money building factories and offices. The government spends on schools, roads, the military and pensions. The rest comes from trade with other countries. When any of these slows down, Americans feel it in jobs and prices.

st.prompt: Which of these makes up the biggest share of the US economy?

options.t: Ordinary people buying goods and services
The government building roads and buying weapons
Selling goods to other countries

st.reveal: Consumer spending, everything households buy, is about two-thirds of US GDP. That's why economists watch shopping so closely. When families cut back, the whole economy feels it.

d.try: For one day, keep a list of every purchase your family makes, even small ones like a bus fare or a packet of biscuits. Next to each, write whether it was a good, like food, or a service, like a haircut. Count which list is longer. In both the USA and India, services are now the bigger part of the economy.
myth: America doesn't make things in factories any more.

Factory jobs have fallen, but the USA is still the world's second-biggest manufacturer after China. Its factories make planes, cars, medicines, chips and machinery, often with more robots and fewer workers than before.

sec.t:
Most Americans work in services: shops, hospitals, banks, schools, restaurants, transport and technology. Factories still make planes, cars, medicines and computer chips, but they use more machines and fewer people than in the past.

Farms employ under 2% of workers, yet the USA is one of the world's biggest exporters of corn and soybeans, thanks to large farms and heavy machinery. Technology companies, many born in [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]] in California, make some of the most valuable businesses on Earth.

Geography helps. The USA has huge areas of farmland, long rivers for shipping, oil and gas, and coasts facing both Europe and Asia. It also draws workers and students from around the world, including many Indian engineers and doctors.

{{story:silicon-valley}}

The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, is the USA's central bank. It was created in 1913 after a series of banking panics. Its main job is to keep prices fairly steady and jobs plentiful. It does this mostly by raising or lowering interest rates, the cost of borrowing.

The US dollar is the most widely used money in the world. Countries trade oil and many other goods in dollars, and central banks across the world keep dollars in reserve. That gives the USA unusual power, and makes the Fed's choices matter far beyond America.

The USA also buys more from other countries than it sells to them, which economists call a trade deficit. It [[import|imports]] phones, clothes, cars and oil, and [[export|exports]] planes, chips, farm crops, films and software. India is an important partner. Indian companies run software services for American firms, and Americans buy Indian medicines, jewellery and clothes. In 2025 the US government raised import taxes, called [[tariff|tariffs]], on goods from many countries, including India, and that set off sharp arguments about trade.

Many big American companies are owned by millions of people who hold small pieces, called shares. They are bought and sold on the [[@stock-market|stock market]], centred on Wall Street in [[@new-york|New York]]. Many families invest their retirement savings there.

When share prices rise, people feel richer and often spend more. When they crash, it can hurt everyone. In 1929 a stock market crash helped trigger the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]], when about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs.

The USA has 50 states, and each sets many of its own rules. The [[federal|federal]] minimum wage has been 7.25 dollars an hour since 2009, but states such as California and Washington set it much higher. California's economy alone would rank among the world's five largest if it were a country.

The economy is rich but uneven. Average income per person is well over 80,000 dollars a year, but the richest families own a large share of the wealth, and many people struggle to afford housing and healthcare. Americans argue fiercely about taxes, trade and how much the government should do. Those debates shape elections every few years.

text: Months come from the Moon. Its shape goes through a full cycle, from new Moon to full Moon and back, in about 29.5 days. People everywhere noticed this, and many early calendars counted time in Moons. The word "month" itself comes from "Moon".

About twelve of these cycles fit into a year of seasons. Twelve Moons make about 354 days, while the Earth takes about 365¼ days to go round the Sun. So twelve months became the standard. Over time, many calendars stretched their months to 30 or 31 days so that twelve of them would fill the solar year exactly.

st.prompt: The Islamic calendar follows only the Moon. What happens to the date of Ramadan in the solar calendar each year?

options.t: It stays on the same date
It moves about 11 days earlier
It moves about a month later

st.reveal: Twelve Moon cycles add up to about 354 days, about 11 days shorter than the solar year. So a calendar that follows only the Moon slips back through the seasons. Ramadan moves through every season over about 33 years.

This story was told in the Middle Ages, but there's no evidence for it. The lengths of the months were mostly set by Julius Caesar's calendar reform, before August got its name.

sec.h: The Moon and the Sun disagree
sec.t:
The trouble is that the Moon and the Sun don't fit together neatly. Twelve Moon cycles fall about 11 days short of a year. Thirteen go about 18 days over.

Different cultures solved this in different ways. The Islamic calendar follows the Moon only, with years of 354 or 355 days. So festivals like [[@eid|Eid]] move about 11 days earlier each year in the solar calendar. Many Hindu, Jewish and Chinese calendars follow the Moon but add an extra month every two or three years to stay in step with the seasons.

The calendar used in most of the world today goes the other way. It ignores the Moon and follows the Sun.

By the time of Julius Caesar, the Roman calendar was a mess. Officials sometimes added extra days to keep friends in power. The months had drifted so far that harvest festivals fell in the wrong season.

In 46 BCE, Caesar added extra days to bring the calendar back in line. That year had about 445 days and was later nicknamed the "year of confusion". From 45 BCE, the new Julian calendar had 365 days, with an extra day every fourth year.

After his death, the month Quintilis was renamed *July* in his honour. Later, Sextilis became *August*, after the first emperor, Augustus.

In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII made a small change to the leap year rule. His Gregorian calendar is the one on most walls today, and it has a [[@leap-years|leap year]] system that keeps it in step with the [[@seasons-why|seasons]] for thousands of years.

But plenty of other calendars are still used side by side. [[@ethiopia|Ethiopia]]'s calendar has 13 months: twelve of 30 days each, and a short thirteenth month of five or six days. India has an official national calendar, along with many regional and religious calendars. Chinese New Year falls on a different date each year, in January or February, because it follows the Moon. That is why people around the world celebrate [[@new-year|the new year]] on so many different days.

text: A banknote is worth something because everyone agrees to accept it. A farmer takes it for rice because she knows a shopkeeper will take it for cloth, and the shopkeeper knows someone else will take it from him. The paper itself is worth almost nothing.

Governments and central banks, like the Reserve Bank of India or the US Federal Reserve, issue money and try to keep its value steady. As long as people trust that a hundred-rupee note will buy roughly the same things next month, the system works. Money is an agreement that has been printed.

It's against the law

st.reveal: Swapping only works if both people want each other's things. Money solves this: everyone accepts it, so you can trade with anyone.

myth: A government could make everyone rich by printing lots more money.

If there is more money but the same amount of food, clothes and other goods, prices simply rise. This is called inflation. In 2009, Zimbabwe printed so much money that it issued a 100-trillion-dollar note, and it still couldn't buy much.

sec.t:
People used many things as money: grain, cattle, salt, cowrie shells and even [[@chocolate-tree|cacao beans]]. The problem with swapping things directly is that you need someone who wants exactly what you have.

Cowries were small, hard to fake and easy to count. They were used as small change in parts of India for hundreds of years, and in West Africa too. Shells that travelled thousands of kilometres along [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] ended up paying for a handful of vegetables.

Look closely at an Indian banknote. It says "I promise to pay the bearer the sum of..." and carries the signature of the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India. For a long time, such promises meant you could swap paper for a fixed amount of gold or silver.

That link has gone. The USA stopped letting other countries swap dollars for gold in 1971. Today, most money isn't paper at all. It is numbers in bank computers, moved by cards or apps such as [[@upi-payments|UPI]]. Banks lend out much of the money people deposit, as explained in [[@money-banks|how banks work]]. The trust is the same. Only the form has changed.

sec.h: Why notes are hard to copy
sec.t:
If anyone could print money at home, nobody would trust it. So banknotes are packed with features that are hard to fake. Indian notes have a watermark of [[@gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]] that shows when held to the light. A security thread changes colour when the note is tilted, and some words are printed so small you need a [[@magnifying-glass|magnifying glass]] to read them.

Raised printing helps people who are blind or have low vision to tell notes apart by touch. US dollars have their own tricks, including colour-shifting ink on the larger notes. Each feature protects the same thing: the trust that makes paper worth something.

*Rupee* comes from the [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] *rūpya*, meaning shaped or stamped silver. In the 1500s, the ruler Sher Shah Suri issued a silver coin called the *rupiya*, an ancestor of today's rupee.

*Dollar* comes from the *thaler*, a silver coin from a valley in today's Czech Republic. Spanish silver coins, also called dollars, were used so widely in the American colonies that the new USA named its own money after them in 1792. Names travel, just like the coins once did.

The Asian Champions Trophy sits between friendly matches and the giant tournaments. It is not a qualifier for the Olympics, but it lets Asia's top sides test new players and tactics against strong rivals.

Hosts take turns. It has been played in China, Japan, Bangladesh, Oman, Malaysia and India. In 2026, India won it in Mohali, [[@punjab|Punjab]], at a stadium named after Balbir Singh Senior, who won three Olympic golds.

Indian [[@hockey-india|hockey]] has a proud history. India won eight Olympic gold medals, six of them in a row from 1928 to 1956, with stars like [[@dhyan-chand|Dhyan Chand]]. In recent years, India won [[@olympics-india|Olympic]] bronze at Tokyo and Paris.

text: Jugglers keep many balls in the air by throwing each one to the same height, at a steady beat. That way, a hand is always empty just before a ball lands in it. Each ball spends most of its time flying, not being held.

The hands do very little work. One throws, the other catches and immediately throws again. A good juggler barely watches the hands at all. Their eyes stay on the top of the arc, where each ball pauses for a split second before it falls.

Expert jugglers look at the top of the arc, where the balls slow down, and track the rest out of the corner of their eye. Some can even juggle three balls blindfolded, using only the feel of each throw.

sec.t:
Almost everyone learns the cascade first. It uses three balls, or any odd number. Each ball crosses from one hand to the other in an arc, making a pattern like a figure eight on its side.

The [[rhythm|rhythm]] goes like this. The right hand throws. When that ball reaches its peak, the left hand throws. When the second ball peaks, the right hand throws again, just before it catches the first ball. The timing never changes. That's why beginners often practise with scarves, which float down slowly and give the brain time to keep up.

With an even number of balls, jugglers usually use a different pattern called the fountain, where each hand looks after its own set of balls.

A ball thrown up slows down, stops for an instant at the top and speeds up on the way down. All balls fall at the same rate, whatever they weigh, because of [[@gravity-fall|gravity]]. A juggler's main job is to make every throw the same height. If one throw goes too low, it arrives early. If it goes too high, it arrives late, and the whole pattern breaks.

More balls means higher throws. To keep five balls going, each must stay in the air longer, so jugglers throw them much higher than three. Every extra ball makes the job a lot harder. That's why the world record is only 11 balls. A juggler named Alex Barron caught 23 throws with 11 balls in 2012.

sec.h: Four thousand years of tossing balls
sec.t:
Juggling is very old. On the wall of a tomb at Beni Hasan in Egypt, painted about 4,000 years ago, women are shown throwing and catching balls, some with arms crossed. Juggling also turns up in ancient China and in Roman writing.

In India, travelling performers called *nats* and street entertainers have juggled balls, knives and flaming torches for centuries, along with tightrope walking. In the 1700s and 1800s, juggling became a star act in the European [[@circus|circus]], and later in American variety shows.

sec.h: What learning does to the brain
sec.t:
In 2004, German scientists taught a group of adults to juggle for three months and scanned their brains. Areas that track moving objects grew slightly. When the people stopped juggling, those areas shrank again.

Most people can learn the cascade in a few days to a few weeks with short, daily practice. You will drop the balls hundreds of times along the way, and every juggler alive has done the same.

text: Video game music is written by composers, much like film music. The big difference is that a game doesn't know in advance what the player will do. You might stand still for ten minutes or race through a level in thirty seconds. So game music has to loop smoothly, change with the action and never become annoying, even after hours of play.

Early game composers worked with tiny computer chips that could make only a few beeps at once. Today they can use full orchestras, [[@choirs|choirs]] and any instrument they like. The challenge is still the same: music that makes the game feel more exciting, scary or beautiful while you play.

st.reveal: Composers often write music in layers that fit together. The game adds or removes layers depending on what is happening, so the music can grow tense in a fight and calm down afterwards without an awkward jump.

Game music is written by trained composers and performed by full orchestras, choirs and bands. Concerts of game music sell out around the world, and since 2023 the Grammy Awards have had a category just for video game soundtracks.

sec.t:
The first arcade games of the 1970s made little more than blips. *Pong* in 1972 had a simple beep when the ball hit a paddle. In 1978, *Space Invaders* added something new: a thumping loop of four low notes that speeds up as the aliens march closer. Players' hearts sped up with it.

[[@tech-game-consoles|Home consoles]] in the 1980s had special sound chips. The Nintendo Entertainment System had just five channels. Two made sharp, buzzy tones, one made a softer tone often used for bass, one made hissing noise for drums, and one could play very short recorded sounds. Composers had to squeeze melody, harmony and [[rhythm|rhythm]] into those five voices. This style is now called chiptune, and some musicians still make it on purpose.

Modern games use what is called adaptive music. Composers write pieces in layers: perhaps strings, then percussion, then brass. When you explore quietly, only the strings play. When an enemy appears, drums fade in. When the fight gets fierce, the brass joins.

Another method switches between sections that are built to join neatly together. Even in 1990, *Super Mario World* added a layer of bongo drums whenever Mario hopped onto his dinosaur friend Yoshi. Players might not notice these tricks, but they feel them. That is how music works on the [[@music-brain|brain]]: it can change your mood before you realise why.

As computers grew more powerful, games could play recorded sound instead of beeps. Composers began writing for real instruments. Many now record with a full [[@orchestra|orchestra]], the same way film scores are made. Others build soundscapes with [[@electronic-music|electronic music]] tools, or mix folk instruments from the world the game is set in.

Game music has also left the screen. Orchestras around the world play concerts of music from series like *Final Fantasy* and *The Legend of Zelda*. In 2011, "Baba Yetu", a song in Swahili written by Christopher Tin for *Civilization IV*, won a Grammy. Since 2023, [[@music-awards|the Grammys]] have had a separate award for the best video game soundtrack.

Music is only half the story. Sound designers create every footstep, sword clang and coin jingle. Some record real objects: crunching celery for breaking bones, or a stretched metal spring for a laser. Others build sounds from scratch on computers.

The best sounds tell players what's going on without a word. A rising chime says "you did something good". A low thud says "watch out". In the history of [[@video-game-history|video games]], a few tiny sounds, like Mario's coin, have become as famous as any song.

text: Zoos began as private collections of rare animals kept by kings and nobles to show off their power and wealth. Over thousands of years they turned into public parks where anyone could pay to see lions, giraffes and bears. In the last hundred years they changed again, with many zoos now saying their main job is protecting animals from [[@extinction-today|extinction]].
The oldest zoo still open is in Vienna, Austria. It started in 1752 in the gardens of an emperor's palace. In India, the first public zoo opened in Madras, now [[@chennai|Chennai]], in 1855.

sec.t:
[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] digging at Hierakonpolis, an ancient Egyptian site, found the graves of animals buried around 3500 BCE, including hippos, baboons and an elephant. Some had healed broken bones, a sign that someone cared for them for years.

Many later rulers kept animals too. Chinese records describe royal parks full of deer and birds. In India, Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] carved rules on stone pillars around 2,200 years ago that protected many kinds of animals from being killed. The Mughal emperors kept cheetahs for hunting, and [[@akbar|Akbar]] is said to have owned hundreds of them.

The idea of a zoo as a place of science grew in Europe in the 1700s and 1800s. In 1828 the Zoological Society of London opened its gardens in Regent's Park, at first only for scientists and members. Londoners began calling it "the zoo", and the short word stuck around the world.

India's zoos followed. Alongside Madras, the Alipore Zoological Gardens in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] opened in 1876. In the USA, the Philadelphia Zoo opened in 1874 and calls itself America's first zoo.

Not everything in that era was kind. Animals were often kept alone in small, bare cages. Some fairs and zoos in Europe and America even displayed people from Africa and Asia, which is now seen as deeply wrong.

{{story:extinction-today}}

In 1907 a German animal dealer named Carl Hagenbeck opened a park near Hamburg with no cages for many animals. Instead, deep ditches called moats kept lions and visitors apart. From the path, it looked as if the animals were roaming free. Zoos around the world copied the idea.

Today good zoos try to give animals space, things to do and company of their own kind. Keepers hide food so animals must search for it, the way they would in the wild.

Some animals exist today because of zoos. The Arabian oryx, a white antelope, was hunted out of the wild by the early 1970s. Zoos bred a herd, and oryx were returned to Oman in 1982. The California condor, a vulture with wings about 3 m across, longer than a car is wide, was saved the same way.

India runs breeding centres too. Zoos and centres help breed vultures, red pandas and the tiny pygmy hog for release.

Not everyone agrees zoos should exist. Critics say large animals such as elephants, which can walk many kilometres a day, suffer in even big enclosures. In 2009, India's Central Zoo Authority told zoos to move their elephants to forest camps and [[sanctuary|sanctuaries]] where possible. Supporters say zoos teach millions of children to care about wildlife they would never otherwise see. Most experts agree that a zoo is only as good as the care it gives.

text: Without bones, your body couldn't hold its shape. Muscles need something firm to pull against, so you couldn't stand, walk or even sit up. You would slump into a soft heap, a bit like a jellyfish washed up on a beach.

You'd also lose protection for your brain, heart and lungs. And you'd lose a hidden blood factory, because the soft marrow inside many bones makes your blood cells. But nature shows there are other ways to build a body. Octopuses, worms and jellyfish have no bones at all, and do just fine.

myth: Bones are dry and dead, like sticks.
Living bones are wet, full of blood vessels and nerves, and constantly being rebuilt. Your skeleton replaces much of itself every ten years or so.

sec.t:
An adult has 206 bones. Babies are born with around 270 to 300, but many fuse together as they grow. The biggest is the thigh bone, or femur. The smallest is the stapes in your ear, about 3 mm long, smaller than a grain of rice.

Bones do three big jobs. They hold you up, like the steel frame inside a tall building. They protect soft parts: your skull guards your brain and your ribs form a cage around your heart and lungs. And they act as [[lever|levers]] for [[@muscles|muscles]], which pull on them to move you.

Inside many bones is soft, jelly-like marrow. It is busy. Every second, it makes about 2 million red [[@blood|blood]] cells, plus white blood cells that fight germs and [[platelet|platelets]] that help cuts heal.

Bones are also your body's calcium bank. About 99 per cent of your calcium is stored in your bones and teeth. When your blood needs more, for your heart to beat properly, the body takes some from your bones.

Without bones, you'd need another blood factory and another calcium store. Your body has neither.

{{story:octopus-smart}}

An octopus has no bones. Its only hard part is a beak, like a parrot's, near the centre of its arms. That means it can pour itself through any gap bigger than its beak, sometimes as small as a coin.

Octopuses are famous for escaping from aquarium tanks. One octopus in New Zealand reportedly slipped through a gap in its tank, slid across the floor and escaped down a drainpipe to the sea. Its arms are made of muscles working against each other, and it can stiffen any part of an arm to make a temporary "elbow" wherever it likes.

Earthworms use a different trick. Their bodies are filled with fluid, divided into many segments. Squeezing muscles in one direction makes a segment long and thin; squeezing the other way makes it short and fat. Waves of this push the worm through soil. Scientists call this a hydrostatic skeleton, a skeleton made of water pressure.

You have some boneless parts that work this way too. Your tongue is a bundle of muscles with no bones, which is why it can curl, flatten and point. So is an elephant's trunk, which has many thousands of muscle bundles and not a single bone.

sec.h: Sharks: bones made of something else
sec.t:
Sharks and rays don't have bones either. Their skeletons are made of [[cartilage|cartilage]], the bendy material in the tip of your nose and your ears. It is lighter than bone. Together with a big oily liver, that helps sharks stay afloat without the air-filled swim bladder most fish use.

Your own skeleton started as cartilage before you were born. Most of it slowly hardened into bone, a process that continues until you're about 25, as you'll find out in how [[@bones-growth|bones grow]].

sec.h: When bones get too little use
sec.t:
Bones grow stronger when you use them. Running, jumping and carrying things make them thicker. Without that, they weaken.

Astronauts in space float, so their legs and spines don't carry weight. Their hips and spines can lose about 1 per cent of their bone mass every month. That's why astronauts on the space station exercise for around two hours a day.

Back on Earth, they can need months of exercise to rebuild. Bones turn out to be one of many surprises in [[@space-body|what space does to the body]], along with puffy faces and growing a little taller.

text: Travelling into the future is possible. In fact it happens all the time, just in tiny amounts. According to [[@einstein|Einstein's]] theories of relativity, time passes more slowly for anything moving very fast, and for anything in strong [[gravity|gravity]]. Astronauts on the space station age very slightly slower than people on the ground.

Travelling into the past is a different story. No experiment has ever shown it, and it causes deep puzzles about cause and effect. A few equations of relativity seem to allow strange shortcuts through time, but most physicists suspect some unknown law forbids them.

myth: Time passes at exactly the same rate for everyone, everywhere.

Einstein showed that time runs slower for things moving very fast and for things deep in strong gravity. The differences are tiny in everyday life but are measured every day by atomic clocks and GPS satellites.

sec.t:
Russian cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev spent a total of 803 days in [[orbit|orbit]]. Because he was moving at about 28,000 km/h, his clock ran a little slow. By the time he retired, he had travelled about 0.02 seconds into the future compared with everyone on Earth.

That doesn't sound like much. But the faster you go, the bigger the effect. A spaceship moving at 99.5 percent of the speed of light would run about ten times slower than Earth. A year aboard would equal about ten years at home. Nobody knows how to build such a ship, but the physics is solid.

Strong gravity slows time as well. Clocks at the top of a mountain tick slightly faster than clocks at sea level. The best atomic clocks can now detect a difference across a height of just a few centimetres.

Near a [[@black-holes|black hole]], the effect becomes enormous. The film Interstellar showed a planet where one hour equalled seven years on Earth. The physicist Kip Thorne, who later won a Nobel Prize, advised the filmmakers so the idea would be based on real equations, though such a planet may not be able to exist.

Going into the past is where science gets slippery. Some solutions to Einstein's equations include wormholes, shortcuts through space and time. A wormhole could, in theory, connect two times as well as two places. But it would need a kind of "exotic matter" with negative energy that nobody has found in usable amounts.

Then there are the paradoxes. If you went back and stopped your grandparents from meeting, you would never be born, so you couldn't go back. Some physicists think the universe would simply prevent such loops. This is the kind of puzzle explored in [[@paradoxes|paradoxes]].

Stephen Hawking, the famous British physicist, liked to test ideas with a sense of humour. On 28 June 2009 he held a party at the University of Cambridge, with balloons and champagne. Only after the date did he send out the invitations. If time travel into the past were possible, he reasoned, someone in the future would read them and drop in. He waited. No guests arrived.

Hawking thought this was a small piece of evidence that backward time travel isn't possible, though he admitted it wasn't a proper experiment. Forward travel is real, but backward travel remains in the land of films and books. Moving yourself across space instantly turns out to be almost as tricky, as you will find in [[@future-teleport|teleportation]].

text: A startup is a young company trying to grow very fast, usually by finding a new way to solve a problem. Most begin with a few founders and very little money. They build a simple version of their product, see if people want it, and change it again and again.

To grow faster than their earnings allow, many startups sell small pieces of the company to investors in return for money. With that cash they hire people, build more and reach more customers. If it works, they may become giants. Most don't make it: the majority close within a few years. The few that succeed can become some of the biggest companies in the world.

st.prompt: An investor gives a startup ₹1 crore and gets 10% of the company in return. What is the whole company now said to be worth?

₹1 crore
₹11 crore

st.reveal: If 10% costs ₹1 crore, then 100% would cost ten times as much, ₹10 crore. This is how startups get their "valuations", though the company may not have earned anywhere near that much yet.

Many famous startups changed their idea completely, which is called a pivot. YouTube began as a dating site and Instagram began as a check-in app. Success usually comes from testing, listening to users and changing course.
