sec.h: From a flat to a giant
sec.t:
In 2007 two former Amazon engineers, Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal (who aren't related), started Flipkart in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]]. At first they sold only books, and they sometimes delivered parcels themselves. Many Indians didn't trust paying online, so Flipkart offered cash on delivery, which became one of its biggest strengths.

Flipkart grew into one of India's largest online shops. In 2018, the American retailer Walmart bought a majority stake for about $16 billion, one of the biggest company deals in India's history.

In 2013 an American investor, Aileen Lee, used the word "[[@myths-unicorns|unicorn]]" for startups worth $1 billion or more, because they seemed so rare. They aren't rare any more. India passed 100 unicorns in 2022, with names like Zerodha, Swiggy, Zomato, Byju's and Paytm among them.

Many startups eventually sell shares to the public on the [[@stock-market|stock market]], an event called an IPO. Others are bought by bigger companies. Some fall back to earth. Byju's, an education company once valued at more than $20 billion, ran into deep money and legal trouble a few years later.

Many successful startups ended up doing something different from what they first planned. YouTube started in 2005 as a site where people could upload dating videos. Instagram began as a check-in app called Burbn. Changing direction like this is called a pivot.

Not every startup needs investors. Zerodha, an Indian share-trading company, grew big without raising outside money, by keeping costs low and charging small fees. This is called bootstrapping.

Startups gather in places with universities, skilled engineers, investors and other founders to learn from. That's why Bengaluru, Delhi's surrounding region and Mumbai lead in India, and why [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]] leads in the United States. In January 2016 the Indian government launched Startup India, offering tax breaks and easier rules. Today India has one of the largest numbers of startups of any country, many now in smaller cities such as [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], Indore and [[@kochi|Kochi]].

text: Jagadish Chandra Bose was a physicist and plant scientist who worked in Calcutta, now Kolkata, about 130 years ago. In the 1890s he built some of the earliest equipment for sending and detecting very short [[@radio-waves|radio waves]], the kind now used in radar, Wi-Fi and [[@5g|5G phones]]. He did this in a small room at his college, often with tools made by a local tinsmith.

Later he turned to plants. Using machines he designed himself, he showed that plants respond to touch, heat and light with tiny electrical signals and movements. That work helped open up the study of how plants sense the world.

st.prompt: Bose built a machine called the crescograph. What did it measure?

options.t: The tiny growth movements of a plant
The strength of earthquakes
The speed of radio waves

st.reveal: The crescograph used a set of levers to magnify a plant's growth about 10,000 times and record it on a smoked glass plate. Bose used it to show how plants respond to light, heat, touch and chemicals.

Try touching a leaf at the tip and at the base. Bose measured the tiny electrical signals that travel through this plant when it folds.
myth: Bose proved that plants feel pain the way animals do.

Bose showed that plants send electrical signals when they are touched, cut or heated, which was a real discovery. But plants have no brain or nerves, and biologists do not think they feel pain as we do. Bose sometimes described his results in ways that went further than his measurements.

sec.h: A teacher who would not be paid less
sec.t:
Bose was born in 1858 in Mymensingh, in what is now [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]]. He studied in Calcutta, then at Cambridge and London. In 1885 he became a professor of physics at Presidency College, Calcutta.

At that time, Indian professors were paid less than British ones for the same job. Bose refused to accept the lower salary, and for three years he taught without taking any pay at all. In the end the college gave in and paid him in full, including the missing years.

In 1894, Bose began experimenting with electric waves after reading about the German scientist Heinrich Hertz. He made waves only a few millimetres to a few centimetres long, far shorter than those used in early radio. He built lenses, [[prism|prisms]] and detectors to bend and catch them.

In a public demonstration in Calcutta, he is reported to have sent waves through walls and a human body to set off a bell some distance away. He also invented sensitive detectors, including one made with a crystal of galena, a lead mineral. His 1904 American patent for it is one of the earliest for a semiconductor device, the family of materials that now fills every computer chip.

Bose chose not to make money from most of his inventions. He believed science should be shared. In 2012 the IEEE, the world's largest engineering society, honoured his millimetre-wave experiments as a landmark in the history of electronics.

{{story:bengali-renaissance}}

Around 1900, Bose noticed that his [[@metal-detectors|metal detectors]] seemed to "tire" and recover, much like a muscle. He wondered whether living things, including plants, behaved in a similar way. He built delicate instruments to find out.

His crescograph magnified a plant's growth about 10,000 times. He showed that [[@plants-move|plants move]] and respond in measurable ways. A touch-me-not leaf folds when a signal passes along it. Shoots slow down when chilled and react quickly to some chemicals. Some of his claims went too far, but modern scientists studying electrical signals in plants often cite his work.

In 1917, Bose opened the Bose Institute in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], one of India's first modern research centres. It still runs today. He was a close friend of the poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]], and the two wrote to each other about science, art and India's future.

Bose also wrote one of the earliest [[@science-fiction|science fiction]] stories in Bengali, about a man who stops a [[cyclone|cyclone]] with a bottle of hair oil. A [[crater|crater]] on the Moon is named after him. The tiny radio waves he studied in a Calcutta classroom now carry phone calls and video in cities across the world.

text: Coding, or programming, means writing instructions that a computer can follow. These instructions are called code, and a set of them that does a job is a program.

Computers can't understand English or Hindi. Deep down, they only understand [[@zero-to-computers|patterns of 0s and 1s]]. So people write code in [[@coding-languages|programming languages]], such as Python, JavaScript or Java, which use English-like words and strict rules. Special programs then translate that code into the 0s and 1s the computer's processor follows.
Every app, website, game and smart device runs on code that somebody wrote, tested and fixed.

st.prompt: A program tells a robot "walk forward 3 steps, turn right, walk forward 3 steps" but the robot crashes into a wall. What is the most likely problem?

options.t: The instructions have a mistake, because the robot did exactly what it was told
The robot decided to disobey
The robot got bored halfway

st.reveal: Computers follow instructions exactly. If the result is wrong, the instructions almost always are too. Programmers call these mistakes bugs, and finding and fixing them is called debugging, which takes up a lot of every coder's day.

d.try: Write instructions for making a jam or chutney sandwich, then hand them to a family member who must follow them exactly, word for word. If you wrote "put jam on the bread" without saying "open the jar" or "use a spoon", they have to stop. Rewrite until it works. That is how programmers think.
myth: You have to be a maths genius to learn coding.

Most everyday programming uses only basic maths. Coding is mainly about breaking problems into small steps, thinking logically and being patient while you fix mistakes. Plenty of children learn it in primary school.
facts: Scratch, a block language for kids

sec.t:
A programming language is a bit like a human language with a very strict [[@grammar-why|grammar]]. Leave out a bracket or misspell a word and the computer refuses to run the program. It can't guess what you meant.

Different languages suit different jobs. Python is popular for science, data and learning to code. JavaScript makes websites interactive. C is used where speed matters, such as in the systems that run phones. Swift and Kotlin are used to build phone [[@apps-made|apps]].

For younger learners, [[@python-scratch|Scratch]], made at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2007, uses colourful blocks that snap together like puzzle pieces, so you can make games without typing.

At its heart, coding means breaking a big job into tiny, exact steps. These step-by-step plans are called [[@algorithms|algorithms]].

Programs use a few basic building blocks. Sequences do one thing after another. Loops repeat steps, such as "do this 100 times". Conditions make choices: "if the player touches a coin, add one point". Variables store information, like a score or a name. With just these pieces, programmers build everything from [[@calculators|calculators]] to [[@video-games|video games]].

Many programmers' first program simply makes the computer display "Hello, world". The tradition was made famous by a 1978 book about the C language.

sec.h: Code that went to the Moon

sec.t:
No one writes perfect code the first time. Mistakes in code are called bugs. A bug might make a game freeze, an app crash or a calculation come out wrong.

Programmers spend much of their time testing their code and hunting for bugs. They read error messages, add checks, and try the program in strange situations to see what breaks. Some say good programming is less about writing code and more about fixing it.

Millions of people write code for a living. India is one of the largest centres of software work in the world. Cities like [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]] and Pune are home to huge numbers of programmers working for Indian and foreign companies. In the USA, [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]] in California is the best-known tech hub.

But coding isn't only for professionals. Scientists use it to study [[climate|climate]] and disease. Artists use it to make music and pictures. Many schools in India and the USA now teach it, and children make their own games with Scratch. Code is a way of giving instructions, and anyone patient enough to learn its rules can write it.

text: Ancient Israel was the land and people of the Israelites, who lived in the hills of Canaan, at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea, about 3,000 years ago. They spoke Hebrew, and over time they came to worship one god alone, which made them unusual among their neighbours. Their stories, laws, poems and history were later gathered into the Hebrew Bible, a book that matters deeply to Jews and that Christians call the Old Testament.

Historians piece together this past from three main sources. One is the Bible itself. Another is the records of powerful neighbours like [[@ancient-egypt|Egypt]], Assyria and [[@babylon|Babylon]]. The third is what [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] dig up: walls, pottery, seals and [[inscription|inscriptions]].

st.prompt: Where was the oldest known mention of the name "Israel" found?

options.t: On a stone carved for an Egyptian pharaoh
In a scroll found in a cave by the Dead Sea
On a coin from ancient Rome

st.reveal: The Merneptah Stele, carved around 1208 BCE, lists peoples that Pharaoh Merneptah claimed to have defeated. One line names "Israel" as a people. It tells us a group called Israel already lived in Canaan by then.

They disagree, sometimes strongly, about earlier events in the Hebrew Bible, such as how large the kingdom of David and Solomon was. Religious believers and scholars may also read these stories in different ways.

d.try: Use a lolly stick or a blunt pencil to carve a short message into a bar of soap, the way ancient people carved inscriptions into stone. Keep it to one line. Notice how much effort each letter takes, and think about why ancient inscriptions are usually short.
myth: Archaeology has either proved the whole Hebrew Bible true or proved it all false.

Neither is the case. Some kings and events, such as King Hezekiah of Judah and the Assyrian attack on his land, appear in outside records too. Other stories have no outside evidence yet, and scholars continue to debate them.
facts: Israel in the north, Judah in the south

sec.h: A name on an Egyptian stone
sec.t:
Around 1208 BCE, Pharaoh Merneptah of Egypt had a large stone slab, or [[stele|stele]], carved to boast of his victories. Near the end, it lists peoples in Canaan he said he had defeated. One line reads, roughly, "Israel is laid waste, its seed is not."

It is the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible. It shows that a people called Israel was living in Canaan by then. It doesn't say how they got there, which is one of the questions scholars still debate.

From about 900 BCE, the picture gets much clearer, because Assyrian and Babylonian records mention Israelite kings by name. Around 722 BCE, the Assyrian [[empire|empire]] conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and moved many of its people away.

Judah survived for a while. King Hezekiah prepared Jerusalem for an Assyrian attack by cutting a tunnel through solid rock to bring water inside the city walls. In 1880, an inscription was found inside the tunnel describing two teams digging from opposite ends until they met. Water still flows through it.

In 587 or 586 BCE, the Babylonians captured Jerusalem and destroyed its temple, known as the First Temple. Many people were taken to Babylon in exile. About 50 years later, the Persian king Cyrus conquered Babylon and allowed exiles to return. They built a new temple, the Second Temple, which stood until the Romans destroyed it in 70 CE.

The Hebrews wrote using an alphabet closely related to the one used by their northern neighbours, the [[@phoenicians|Phoenicians]]. Later they switched to a square script borrowed from Aramaic, the ancestor of the Hebrew letters used today.

In 1947, Bedouin shepherds exploring caves near Qumran, by the [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]], found clay jars full of ancient scrolls. These Dead Sea Scrolls, written over about 300 years before and around the time of Jesus, include the oldest known copies of books of the [[@bible-intro|Hebrew Bible]]. They showed that the text had been copied with great care for more than a thousand years.

The traditions of ancient Israel shaped Judaism, and through it influenced Christianity and Islam, which also honour figures such as Abraham and Moses. Billions of people today belong to these faiths.

Jewish communities spread across the world, including to India. The Cochin Jews lived on the Kerala coast for many centuries, and the Paradesi Synagogue in [[@kochi|Kochi]], built in 1568, is still in use. The Bene Israel of Maharashtra have their own long history in India too.

text: The Harlem Renaissance was a time, roughly from the end of the [[@world-war-one|First World War]] to the mid-1930s, when Black American artists, writers and musicians created a huge amount of new work. Its home was Harlem, a neighbourhood in northern Manhattan in [[@new-york|New York]].

*Renaissance* means rebirth. People used the word because the movement felt like a new beginning for Black culture in America. Poets like [[@langston-hughes|Langston Hughes]] wrote about everyday Black life with pride. Jazz musicians packed the clubs. Thinkers argued that art could help win respect and equal rights.

Only Black customers
Anyone who could pay

st.reveal: Even in Harlem, the Cotton Club served white audiences, while the musicians and dancers on stage were Black. It shows how even this golden age happened inside a segregated country.

myth: The Harlem Renaissance was mainly about music.
Jazz was a big part of it, but writers, poets, painters, photographers, thinkers and actors were just as important. It was a movement across many arts at once.

sec.t:
The story starts in the American South. After slavery ended, Southern states passed unfair laws that kept Black people from voting and separated them in schools, trains and restaurants. Violence was common, and farm work paid very little.

From about 1910, millions of Black Americans moved north to cities such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, looking for factory work and more freedom. Historians call this the Great Migration. Between 1910 and 1970, about six million people made the journey, often by train, carrying their music, food and stories with them. Harlem, with its fine brownstone houses, became the biggest Black neighbourhood in the country. People came from the South and from Caribbean islands such as Jamaica, bringing new voices and ideas.

Harlem's nights belonged to [[@jazz|jazz]]. Duke Ellington led his orchestra at the Cotton Club. Louis Armstrong's trumpet and Bessie Smith's voice filled theatres and record players. Dances like the Lindy Hop were born in Harlem's ballrooms, especially the Savoy, where Black and white dancers could dance together.

Painters joined in too. Aaron Douglas created bold [[mural|murals]] using silhouettes and African designs. Photographer James Van Der Zee recorded Harlem families and weddings, and his pictures are now a priceless record of the time.

W. E. B. Du Bois edited *The Crisis*, the magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It published many young writers for the first time. Du Bois was interested in struggles beyond America too. His 1928 novel *Dark Princess* tells of an alliance between a Black American man and an Indian princess working against [[empire|empire]].

The [[@great-depression|Great Depression]] that began in 1929 hit Harlem very hard. Money for books, plays and nightclubs dried up, and many people lost their jobs. A riot in 1935, sparked by anger over poverty and unfair treatment, is often seen as the end of the era.

Its influence never faded, though. The writers and musicians of Harlem inspired the [[@civil-rights|civil rights movement]] of the 1950s and 1960s, and later poets such as [[@maya-angelou|Maya Angelou]]. The Apollo Theater, which began hosting Black performers in 1934, still runs its famous Amateur Night today.

text: The Nazca lines are giant drawings scratched into the desert of southern [[@peru|Peru]]. There are straight lines running for kilometres, triangles and spirals, and pictures of animals: a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider, a whale. They were made by the Nazca people, who lived there roughly 2,000 years ago, between about 500 BCE and 500 CE.

We know how they made them. They moved the dark stones on the surface to show the paler ground underneath. Why they made them is less certain. Most [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] think the lines were part of religious ceremonies, perhaps walked along like sacred paths, and many seem linked to water, which was precious in the desert.

st.prompt: How did the Nazca people make lines that have lasted about 2,000 years?

options.t: They moved dark surface stones aside to show lighter ground underneath
They painted the ground with white clay
They dug deep trenches and filled them with sand

st.reveal: The desert is covered in reddish-brown stones. Lift them away and the paler, yellowish soil below shows through. In one of the driest places on Earth, with almost no wind or rain to disturb them, the lines have survived.

d.try: Make a giant drawing like the Nazca people. On a beach, a sandy patch or a playground with chalk, sketch a small animal on paper first, then divide it into a grid. Scale each square up using string and sticks. Then look at it from a window or high step, and see if it's still recognisable.

Many figures can be seen from the surrounding hills. In 1982 a small team recreated a large Nazca bird in a few days using only wooden stakes and string. The Nazca people had everything they needed.
facts: the Nazca people, about 500 BCE to 500 CE

sec.t:
The Nazca desert floor is covered with small stones, stained reddish-brown by iron over time. Just below is lighter, yellowish soil. Rake the stones aside into neat edges and a pale line appears.

The desert is one of the driest places on Earth, gets almost no rain and has little wind at ground level. So the lines have barely changed for centuries. The hummingbird is about 93 metres long, nearly the length of a football field. The monkey has a curly tail and nine fingers.

Early researchers thought the lines might be a giant calendar pointing to the stars. When scientists checked, only a few lines lined up with the Sun or stars, no more than chance would give.

Today, most experts favour ideas tied to [[ritual|ritual]]. Some lines appear to have been walked many times, worn down by feet. Others point towards water sources or mountains, where rain came from. Broken pots found at the ends of some lines suggest offerings were left there. The Nazca relied on underground channels for water, and rain was a matter of life and death.

The Nazca people lived in the dry river valleys of southern Peru many centuries before the Inca. They were skilled farmers. The spiralling wells and underground channels they built to reach water, called puquios, still supply some farms today.

They were superb artists too. Nazca potters painted bowls and jars in many colours, with the same hummingbirds, monkeys, killer whales and fierce mythical beings that appear on the desert floor. Their weavers made fine cloth. The Nazca culture faded around 500 to 600 CE, perhaps partly because of floods, [[drought|droughts]] and the cutting of trees that had held the valley soil together.

Archaeologists keep finding more. Many smaller figures, drawn along footpaths, are faint and easy to miss. In 2024, a team from Yamagata University in Japan trained [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] on photos of known figures, then let it search aerial images. With the help of [[@drones|drones]] and fieldwork, they confirmed 303 new figures in about six months, including people, cats and llamas.

[[archaeology|Archaeology]] doesn't need aliens to explain the lines. In 1982 a small team recreated a big Nazca bird in a few days, using just stakes and string. And the strangest part? The dry desert that saved these drawings isn't even the driest in South America. That record belongs to Chile's Atacama, next door, one of the [[@extreme-driest|driest places on Earth]].

text: The [[@weather-records|coldest places]] where people live all year round are two villages in Siberia, Russia: Oymyakon and Verkhoyansk. Both have recorded temperatures of about minus 68 °C, and both claim the title.

These are proper settlements, with homes, schools and shops, not research stations. In January, the average temperature in Oymyakon is around minus 50 °C. Far colder temperatures have been measured in Antarctica, but nobody lives there permanently. Places like Yakutsk, Siberia's big city, and towns in Alaska, northern [[@canada|Canada]] and Greenland also get bitterly cold, and people manage there too.

st.prompt: In the US, temperatures are often given in Fahrenheit. At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same number?

st.reveal: Minus 40 °C is exactly minus 40 °F. Places like Oymyakon and Alaska often get colder than that in winter, so locals there don't need to say which scale they mean.

myth: Dras in Ladakh is the second-coldest inhabited place in the world.
Dras is one of the coldest places in India, with winter nights often far below freezing. But towns in Siberia, northern Canada and Alaska regularly get much colder, so it is nowhere near second.

sec.t:
Oymyakon and Verkhoyansk sit in deep valleys in the Sakha Republic, also called Yakutia, in eastern [[@russia|Russia]]. In winter, cold heavy air slides down from the mountains and pools in the valleys, like water collecting at the bottom of a bowl. With almost no wind and long nights, the cold just builds.

Verkhoyansk recorded about minus 67.8 °C in 1892. Oymyakon recorded about minus 67.7 °C in 1933, though some reports suggest even lower figures. A large sign in Oymyakon calls it the "Pole of Cold". Oymyakon is home to about 500 people.

sec.h: Even colder, but nobody lives there
sec.t:
The coldest air temperature ever measured at a weather station was minus 89.2 °C, at Vostok Station in [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] on 21 July 1983. [[@satellites-help|Satellites]] have since detected surface temperatures below minus 90 °C in hollows on the high Antarctic ice.

At those temperatures, breathing outside without covering your mouth would hurt your lungs. Scientists at Vostok come and go in shifts. Nobody makes a permanent home there.

The lowest temperature ever recorded in the United States was about minus 62 °C (minus 80 °F) at Prospect Creek, in [[@alaska|Alaska]], in January 1971. Towns in Alaska, such as Fairbanks, often see minus 40 in winter.

In the lower 48 states, a few small towns compete for the nickname "Icebox of the Nation", including International Falls, Minnesota, and Fraser, Colorado.

India's coldest inhabited places are high in the Himalayas. Dras, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], lies about 3,300 m above sea level, and its winter nights are often well below minus 20 °C. Snow can cut it off from the rest of India for months.

Leh, Kargil and [[@spiti|villages in Spiti]], in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], also face long, freezing winters. People there use thick mud-brick walls, wood and dung stoves, and warm woollen clothes to stay comfortable. Your body has its own tricks for cold, such as shivering and the [[@goosebumps|goosebumps]] left over from furrier ancestors.

text: Kutch, in the far west of Gujarat, is the largest district in India. Much of it is the Rann, a flat salt desert that floods in the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. Life there was always hard, and people turned what little they had into beautiful, useful things.

The result is one of the richest craft regions on Earth. Kutch is known for Ajrakh block printing, Rogan painting, mirror-studded [[embroidery|embroidery]], Bandhani tie-dye, mud-and-mirror wall art called lippan, woven shawls and blankets, and copper-coated bells. Many crafts belong to particular communities, and skills pass from parents to children.

options.t: They fold the cloth and press it, printing a mirror copy
They hold the cloth up to a mirror and trace it
A second artist copies it by eye

st.reveal: The thick castor-oil paint stays wet for a while. Folding the cloth in half and pressing it gently prints a perfect mirror image of the pattern on the other side.

sec.h: Painting with oil and a stick
sec.t:
In the village of Nirona, a few artists practise Rogan painting. They boil castor oil for many hours until it turns thick and sticky, then mix in coloured powders. The artist puts a blob of paste in one palm and draws it out into thin threads with a metal stick, laying the thread on cloth. No brush touches the fabric.

Often only half the design is painted. The cloth is folded and pressed, printing a [[@mirrors|mirror]] copy on the other half. Rogan nearly died out in the last century. One family in Nirona kept it alive for generations, and they now train more learners.

On 26 January 2001, a powerful [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] struck Kutch. Thousands of people died and the city of Bhuj was badly damaged. But many of the region's round mud huts, called bhungas, stayed standing. Their circular shape and light roofs helped them sway instead of cracking.

Inside a bhunga, the walls are often covered in lippan kaam. Women shape raised patterns from clay mixed with dung, then press in small pieces of mirror. When a lamp is lit at night, the whole room twinkles. Lippan is now made on boards to hang in city homes too.

sec.h: Threads that tell who you are
sec.t:
Kutch has more than a dozen styles of embroidery. Rabari, Ahir, Jat, Meghwal and other communities each use their own stitches, colours and [[motif|motifs]]. Someone who knows the styles can often tell where a woman comes from just by looking at her blouse or her quilt. Tiny round mirrors, called abhla, are stitched into many designs to catch the light.

In Bhujodi, families of weavers make shawls and blankets on pit looms, some from wool of local sheep and camels. Nearby, Bandhani makers tie thousands of tiny knots in cloth before dyeing it, and a single fine sari can hold tens of thousands of dots.

Back in Nirona and the nearby village of Zura, metalworkers make bells for cattle and camels. They fold a sheet of iron into shape, coat it in copper and brass powder, wrap it in mud and bake it in a fire. The coating melts and fuses to the bell. Each one is tuned by tapping, and herders say they can tell their own animals' bells apart in the dark.

Every winter, a tent city rises on the white salt of the [[@gujarat-rann|Rann]] for the Rann Utsav festival, and visitors come to buy these crafts straight from the people who made them. The salt itself is a strange sight: under a full moon, the desert glows almost as white as snow.

text: Lakshadweep is a group of 36 small coral islands in the Arabian Sea, off the coast of [[@kerala|Kerala]]. Only 10 of them have people living on them. They are flat and low, fringed with white coral sand and [[@coconut|coconut palms]], and surrounded by calm, clear [[lagoon|lagoons]] of turquoise water. Beyond the lagoons, waves crash on the reefs.

It is India's smallest union [[territory|territory]]. All the islands together cover only about 32 square km, and about 64,000 people lived there at the 2011 [[census|census]]. Most islanders fish, grow coconuts or work for the local government. Visitors need a special permit, which helps protect the islands and their way of life.

st.prompt: How did most of Lakshadweep's islands form?

options.t: From coral reefs that grew on top of old, sunken volcanic rock
From lava pouring out of active volcanoes
From sand dumped by rivers flowing out of India

st.reveal: Most are coral atolls. Corals built reefs on top of old volcanic rock that slowly sank. As the rock went down, the corals kept growing upwards towards the light, leaving rings of reef and small islands of coral sand.

They are on opposite sides of India. Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea, west of Kerala. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are far away in the Bay of Bengal, to the east.

sec.t:
The [[@coral-reefs|reefs]] are full of life: parrotfish, butterflyfish, octopuses, [[@ocean-sea-cucumbers|sea cucumbers]] and reef sharks. Green and hawksbill turtles graze on seagrass in the lagoons. The waters around the islands are also rich in tuna.

Lakshadweep fishers are known for catching skipjack tuna by pole and line. They throw small live bait fish into the water to draw a tuna shoal close, then pull the fish up one by one on hooks. It catches fewer unwanted animals than big nets do, and has been practised here for generations. Much of the catch is boiled, smoked and dried into a hard fish called masmin, sold in Kerala and beyond.

Most islanders are Muslim, and Islam is thought to have reached the islands many centuries ago through traders and preachers sailing from Arabia and Kerala. The main language is a form of [[@malayalam|Malayalam]] called Jeseri. On Minicoy, the southernmost island, people speak Mahl, a language closely related to Dhivehi, which is spoken in the nearby Maldives.

Life follows the [[rhythm|rhythm]] of the sea and the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. Coconut is everywhere: in food, in rope made from its fibre, and in the thatch of older houses. Kavaratti, the capital, has a famous mosque with carved wooden ceilings. Minicoy has a tall lighthouse built by the British in 1885.

Low coral islands are some of the places most at risk from a warming planet. When the sea gets too hot, corals throw out the tiny [[algae|algae]] living inside them and turn white. This is called [[@coral-bleaching|coral bleaching]], and it hit Lakshadweep's reefs hard in 1998, 2010 and 2016. Some reefs recovered. Others did not.

Rising sea levels are another worry, because the islands have no high ground. Healthy reefs act as natural breakwaters, taking the force of waves before they reach the shore. Protecting the corals helps protect the islands themselves. The government also limits tourism and fresh water use, because the islands depend on rain and on a thin layer of fresh groundwater floating above the salty sea water underground.

text: There isn't one single Buddhist book. Instead there are several large collections, each treasured by a different branch of Buddhism. All of them hold teachings said to come from [[@buddha|the Buddha]], the Indian teacher who lived about 2,500 years ago. They also contain rules for monks and nuns, poems, stories and explanations by later scholars.

The oldest complete collection is the Pali Canon, used in [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. Other traditions, especially in China, Japan, Korea and Tibet, use bigger collections that include many texts first written in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]].

st.prompt: How were the Buddha's teachings kept safe for the first few hundred years?

options.t: Monks memorised them and chanted them together
They were carved on stone pillars
They were written on palm leaves from the very start

st.reveal: Groups of monks learned long texts by heart and recited them in unison, so any slip by one person was easy to catch. The tradition says they were first written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE.

n.certNote: Buddhists of different traditions accept different collections as scripture. Historians also debate how much of the oldest texts goes back to the Buddha's own words and how much was added by later teachers.

myth: Buddhism has one holy book, the way many people think of the Bible or the Quran.

Different Buddhist traditions use different collections. Theravada Buddhists follow the Pali Canon, while Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Tibetan Buddhists use much larger collections with many more sutras.
facts: the Pali Canon, or Tipitaka (three baskets)

sec.t:
According to Buddhist tradition, soon after the Buddha died, about 500 monks met at Rajagriha, today's Rajgir in Bihar. His close companion Ananda recited the teachings he had heard, and another monk, Upali, recited the rules for monastic life. The others listened, checked and agreed.

For centuries after that, nobody wrote these teachings down. Groups of monks memorised them and chanted them together, often in patterns of repeated lines that made them easier to remember. Many monks today can still recite hours of text from memory.

The Pali Canon is also called the *Tipitaka*, meaning "three baskets". The first basket, the Vinaya, holds rules for monks and nuns, down to how to wear robes and share food. The second, the Sutta, holds the Buddha's talks and conversations. The third, the Abhidhamma, carefully analyses the mind.

Tradition says the canon was first written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE, on dried palm leaves. Inside the Sutta basket are some of the most loved Buddhist writings. The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses about living wisely. The [[@jataka-tales|Jataka tales]] are stories of the Buddha's past lives, often as a monkey, an elephant or a deer.

Some of the oldest Buddhist [[manuscript|manuscripts]] known are fragile scrolls of birch bark from Gandhara, in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan. They are about 2,000 years old and are now kept at the British Library in London.

The British Library also holds a copy of the Diamond Sutra found in a cave at Dunhuang in western China. It was [[@printing-press|printed]] from carved wooden blocks in 868 CE, and it carries the date, which makes it the oldest dated printed book known. In Mandalay, Myanmar, the whole Pali Canon was carved onto 729 marble slabs in the 1860s, each in its own small shrine. People call it the world's largest book.

In 1881 the Pali Text Society was founded in London to print the Pali Canon in the Roman alphabet, along with English translations. Today the texts are printed in Sinhala, Burmese, Thai and Devanagari scripts too, and much of the canon can be read free online.

In [[monastery|monasteries]] from Sri Lanka to Japan, monks still chant passages every morning and evening, and lay Buddhists listen at festivals and funerals. Many children in Theravada countries learn short Pali verses by heart, just as young monks did more than 2,000 years ago.

text: A journalist finds out what is happening and tells the public about it, clearly and truthfully. Some report on cricket matches or floods. Others spend months digging into secrets that powerful people would rather hide.

The job sounds simple, but the hard part is being sure. A reporter collects facts by watching, asking questions, reading documents and checking with several people. An editor then asks, "How do we know this?" Only when the answer is solid does the story go out in a newspaper, on television, on the radio or online.

st.prompt: In a news report, where do journalists usually put the most important facts?

options.t: In the very first sentence or two
In the last paragraph, as a surprise
Spread evenly through the whole story

st.reveal: Reporters use the "inverted pyramid". The biggest facts go at the top and the details come after. Editors used to cut long stories from the bottom to fit the page, so the key news had to be first.

myth: Journalists can print anything they hear as long as they say "sources say".
Good newsrooms check facts with more than one source, ask the people involved for their side and correct mistakes publicly. Printing false and harmful claims about a person can break the law.

sec.t:
Every reporter learns six questions: who, what, where, when, why and how. A good news story answers most of them in the first few lines. That style is called the inverted pyramid, with the biggest facts at the wide top and smaller details below.

Journalists also try to keep facts and opinions apart. A news report says what happened. An opinion column, clearly marked, says what the writer thinks about it. Mixing the two quietly is one way readers get misled, along with tricks like [[@statistics-lies|numbers used carelessly]].

Some of the most famous journalism is investigative. In 1972 two young reporters at the *Washington Post*, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, began following a small story about a break-in at the Watergate building in Washington DC. It led to the US president's own team. In 1974 President Richard Nixon resigned.

In 1887 Nellie Bly pretended to be ill so she could be sent to a New York asylum for women. Her reports on the cruel conditions there led to changes. New York City put more money into caring for patients after her stories appeared. Two years later she went round the world in 72 days, beating the 80 days in Jules Verne's novel.

In India, freedom of the press is protected as part of the right to free speech in the Constitution. In the USA it is written into the First Amendment. Both countries also have laws against spreading false, damaging claims about people.

Good journalists protect people who give them information in secret. They admit and correct their mistakes. In India, the [[@right-to-information|Right to Information]] law lets anyone, including reporters, ask government offices for records.

Today anyone with a phone can post a video of something happening. That helps reporters see events they missed. It also spreads rumours fast, which is why careful checking matters more than ever. Many [[@jobs-journalist-day|newsrooms]] now have fact-checking teams that test viral posts and photos before anyone treats them as news.

Children can do journalism too. Many schools in India and the USA have student newspapers. Young reporters learn the same lesson as the professionals: ask, check, then write, and spot [[@fake-news|fake news]] before you pass it on.

text: Sangam poetry is the oldest known body of Tamil literature. It is a collection of about 2,400 poems, written by more than 470 named poets, and many unnamed ones, roughly 2,000 years ago. The poets included kings, farmers, potters, merchants and women.

The poems are short and sharp, full of real places, plants and animals. Some describe falling in love, missing someone or quarrelling. Others praise brave kings, mourn heroes or scold rulers who were mean with money. The name comes from *sangam*, meaning "gathering", after a legend that poets met in academies at Madurai under the Pandya kings.

st.prompt: In Sangam love poems, a seashore setting usually goes with which feeling?

options.t: Anxious waiting for someone who has gone away
The first happy meeting of lovers
Anger and war

st.reveal: Each landscape matched a mood. The mountains went with lovers meeting, and the seashore with anxious waiting, often for a fisherman out at sea. Readers who knew the code could feel the mood as soon as a poem named a crab, a boat or a seashore flower.

src: Ramanujan A. K. (1985), Poems of Love and War. Columbia University Press.

src.Zvelebil K. (1973), The Smile of Murugan: On Tamil Literature of South India. Brill.

n.certNote: Scholars agree the poems are very old, but their exact dates are debated. Most place them roughly between 300 BCE and 300 CE, and the story of three Sangam academies in Madurai is treated as legend.

myth: Sangam poems are all about gods and religion.

Most Sangam poems are about ordinary human life. They describe love, loneliness, friendship, farming, war, generosity and grief, with very few prayers. Religious Tamil poetry became much more common in later centuries.

sec.t:
Sangam poems fall into two big groups. *Akam*, meaning "inside", poems are about love and private feelings. They rarely name the lovers. Instead, they speak in voices like "the girl", "her friend" or "the mother", so any reader can step into the scene.

*Puram*, meaning "outside", poems are about public life: battles, kings, generosity, death and fame. One famous puram poem, by Kaniyan Pungundranar, opens with the line usually translated as "Every town is our town, everyone our kin". It goes on to say that good and bad do not come from others, and is still quoted in speeches today.

One of the best known Sangam love poems, from an anthology called Kuruntokai, compares two lovers to rain falling on red earth. The poet says their parents were strangers, and they themselves had never met, yet their hearts mixed together like the red soil and the water. The translator A. K. Ramanujan made it famous in English under the title "Red Earth and Pouring Rain".

The poem is only five lines long. Like a [[@haiku|haiku]], it uses one clear picture to say something big. Many Sangam poems work this way, and that is one reason modern readers find them so fresh.

For centuries, Sangam poems survived on palm-leaf [[manuscript|manuscripts]], copied by hand in [[monastery|monasteries]] and family homes. Palm leaves rot, crack and get eaten by insects. By the 1800s, some poems were almost forgotten.

The scholar U. V. Swaminatha Iyer spent decades travelling from village to village in Tamil Nadu, searching for these manuscripts. He compared copies line by line, fixed copying mistakes and printed many of the anthologies for the first time. Tamil readers still remember him with great respect for it.

Sangam poetry tells historians about ancient Tamil life: trade with Rome, the [[@cholas|Chola]], Chera and Pandya kingdoms, farming, food and festivals. It also shaped later Tamil literature, including the [[@thirukkural|Thirukkural]].

In 2004, Tamil became the first language to be declared a classical language by the Government of India, and the Sangam poems were a big part of the reason. They are still taught in schools, set to music and quoted at weddings. A poem written two thousand years ago can still say exactly what a person feels today.

text: A translator turns writing in one language into another. An interpreter does the same for speech or sign language, often live. Both need to understand two languages and two cultures very well.

The job isn't swapping words. Translators read a whole sentence or paragraph, work out what it means and how it feels, and then write it again as a native speaker would. A joke must stay funny, a sad poem sad and a legal contract exact. That takes judgement, research and many small decisions.

d.try: Pick a saying from a language you speak at home, like Hindi's "naach na jaane, aangan tedha" (she can't dance, so she blames the crooked courtyard). Translate it word for word into English, then find an English saying that means the same thing. Which version would you choose?
myth: A good translation swaps each word for the matching word in the other language.
Languages put words together differently and use different idioms. Good translators carry over meaning, tone and feeling, which often means changing the words quite a lot.

sec.t:
Languages don't match word for word. Hindi has separate words for your father's brother (chacha) and your mother's brother (mama), while English has only "uncle". Some languages, like Turkish, can build what English says in a whole sentence into one long word.

[[@idioms|Idioms]] are the biggest trap. If a Hindi speaker says "naach na jaane, aangan tedha", the words mean "she can't dance and says the courtyard is crooked". The meaning is "blaming your tools for your own mistakes". A translator into English might use "a bad workman blames his tools".

Tone matters too. Hindi has three ways to say "you" (tu, tum and aap), from very close to very polite. English has only one. A translator must find other ways to show how polite or rude a character is being.

Interpreters work with speech, so they can't stop to look things up. In "consecutive" interpreting, the speaker pauses every few sentences. In "simultaneous" interpreting, the interpreter speaks almost at the same time as the speaker, usually from a soundproof booth, a few words behind.

Simultaneous interpreting was first used on a large scale at the Nuremberg trials in 1945 and 1946, when Nazi leaders were tried after the war. Courtroom speeches were interpreted live into English, French, Russian and German through [[@sound-recording|headphones]]. Today the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] works in six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.

Sign language interpreters do the same job between spoken and [[@sign-language|signed languages]], which have their own [[@grammar-why|grammar]].

In 1954, an IBM computer in New York translated about 60 Russian sentences into English. People predicted machines would replace translators within a few years. It took much longer.

Modern [[@translation-apps|translation apps]] use [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] trained on huge numbers of texts that already exist in two languages. They are now very useful for menus, signs and quick messages. But they can still miss jokes, tone, culture and context. For books, films, medicine and law, human translators usually check and correct machine translations, or do the work themselves.

In a country like India, with 22 languages listed in the Constitution, translators help people read each other's literature and understand each other's laws. Every film that is dubbed or subtitled, every [[@dubbing-subtitles|Hindi film shown in Tamil]], has a translator behind it.

text: A food truck is a small kitchen built inside a van or lorry. It has a stove or grill, a fridge, a sink and a hatch in the side where customers order. The cooks drive to a busy spot, such as an office area at lunchtime, a college gate or a park on a Sunday, open the hatch and start serving.
The big advantage is that the kitchen moves. A restaurant has to wait for people to walk in. A food truck can go where the crowds are, and change its spot from one day to the next.

sec.h: Fitting a restaurant into a van
sec.t:
Space is the hardest problem. The cooking area is often only 3–5 metres long, about the length of a car, and two or three people work inside it. Everything is planned so that a cook can reach the fridge, the grill and the serving window with a step or two.

Power comes from a [[@electricity-made|generator]], from gas cylinders, or from a plug point when the truck is parked somewhere with electricity. Most trucks carry two water tanks: one for clean water and one for the grey water that comes out of the sink. A small menu helps too. A truck selling six dishes needs far fewer ingredients than a restaurant selling sixty.

For years, trucks in the USA had a reputation for cheap, dull food. Then, in 2008, a cook named Roy Choi started a truck in Los Angeles that sold Korean [[@bbq|barbecue]] folded into [[@tacos|tacos]]. The truck kept moving, so the team posted its location on Twitter. Crowds followed it around the city.

Other cooks copied the idea. Soon there were trucks selling dumplings, dosas and gourmet [[@burgers-hotdogs|burgers]], and finding the truck became part of the fun. Indian cities such as Bengaluru, Pune and Delhi saw a wave of food trucks in the 2010s, often run by young people who could not afford a full restaurant.

A food truck has to follow two sets of rules: the ones for food and the ones for vehicles. In India, food businesses need a licence or registration from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. In the USA, each city has its own permits, and some cities limit how many trucks may operate, so there can be long waiting lists.

Then there is parking. Many cities say where trucks can stop and for how long, so they don't block traffic or crowd the doors of restaurants that pay rent. The best spot in town is worth a lot, and truck owners sometimes arrive before sunrise to get it.

A truck costs much less than a restaurant to start, so a cook can test a new idea without borrowing huge sums. If a dish doesn't sell in one neighbourhood, the truck can try another. Customers tell the cook what they think right at the window, which is faster feedback than any survey. The hard part is the long day: shopping at dawn, cooking for hours in a hot metal box, then cleaning every surface before driving home. Several famous restaurants began as a single truck with a handwritten menu taped to the window.

text: People have bought cooked food from shops, inns and stalls for thousands of years. But a restaurant in the modern sense, where you sit at your own table, choose from a menu and pay for what you order, is newer. Cities in Song [[dynasty|dynasty]] China had places like this by about 900 years ago. In Europe, they took off in Paris in the 1760s.
The word itself is French. A *restaurant* was first a nourishing broth that "restored" your strength. Shops selling it began to call themselves restaurants, and the name stuck.

sec.t:
For most of history, eating out meant eating whatever was cooking. Travellers stopped at inns, where the owner served one meal at a fixed time on a shared table. If you arrived late, you went hungry. In towns, stalls and taverns sold cheap food and drink. Roman towns had street counters for hot meals, and Indian cities had sweet shops and food sellers, as they still do.

What these places usually lacked was choice. There was no menu, no separate table for your family and no promise that the food would be ready whenever you came.

In the 1760s, a few Paris shops started selling bouillon, a rich meat broth, to customers who felt delicate. Unlike inns, they let people come at any time, sit at small separate tables and choose from a written list of dishes with prices. That list was an early menu.

The idea spread fast. After the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]] of 1789, some cooks who had worked for noble families opened restaurants of their own. By the early 1800s, Paris had hundreds of them, and the French word spread to languages all over the world.

Spain has an even older survivor. Sobrino de Botín in Madrid has served roast meats since 1725, and Guinness World Records lists it as the oldest restaurant still running. Its owners say the wood-fired oven has hardly gone out in three centuries.

In New York, the Delmonico brothers, immigrants from Switzerland, opened a café in 1827 and later a grand restaurant. Delmonico's offered printed menus, tablecloths and a wide choice of dishes, which was a new experience for Americans used to taverns. Over the next century, diners, cafeterias and family restaurants spread across the USA, leading eventually to the [[@fast-food-history|fast food]] chains of the 1950s.

In India, eating out has a long history at temples, festivals and food stalls. Modern restaurants grew in the late 1800s and early 1900s, often called "hotels" even when they offered no rooms. Cooks from Udupi in Karnataka opened vegetarian restaurants serving [[@dosa-idli|dosas and idlis]] in cities across India. The Mavalli Tiffin Room, or MTR, opened in Bengaluru in 1924 and still has queues on weekend mornings.

In Mumbai and Pune, Persian migrants from Iran started Irani cafés with bentwood chairs, marble tables and bun maska with chai. A few of these cafés, more than a century old, still serve the same breakfasts. Veeraswamy, opened in London in 1926, is often called the oldest surviving Indian restaurant in Britain.
